IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.            OF 2026
[@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 10321 OF 2025)
 
SUSHILA TRIPATHI   … APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR  … RESPONDENTS
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant’s husband was a freedom fighter, he
took part in the Maihar Praja Mandal Movement of 1945-46
and was lodged in Maihar Jail. His claim for Samman Nidhi
(freedom fighter’s pension ) could not be realised during
his  lifetime.  His  widow’s  claim  for  recognition  and
honour of her husband’s and her family's sacrifices has
reached this Court after a long-drawn contest.1
2.1 The  freedom  we  exercise  and  the  constitutional
institutions  through  which  we  govern  ourselves  are  the
inheritance  of  a  struggle  sustained  by  ordinary  men  and
women.  Their  contribution  cannot  be  measured  by  the
1  This appeal is preferred against the order dated 14.02.2025 passed
by High Court by which the Division Bench allowed the appeal of the
respondents and set aside the order dated 05.01.2023 of learned Single
Judge.
1

--- Page 63 ---
prominence of their names in public memory. In our view,
the  grant  of  Samman  Nidhi discharges  an  obligation  of
gratitude that has its source in the Constitution itself. That
obligation  is  one  of  recognition,  not  compensation.  It  is
owed equally to the known and the unknown participants of
the freedom struggle, and it reaches the families who bore
the cost of their sacrifice.
2.2 We must understand how this obligation of gratitude
takes  its  shape.  Gratitude,  unlike  compensation,  is  not
measured by an account of what was lost. The cost of the
sacrifice it honours was borne not by the freedom fighter
alone, but by the family. And that sacrifice was made by men
and women who expected nothing in return, and therefore
kept  no  account  of  it.  The  household  lost  its  earning
member, children their schooling, and elders their care. The
nation received the benefit, while it was often the families
who  bore  the  cost.  These  sacrifices  must  translate  into
expressions of gratitude and continued acknowledgement of
debt owed to the families.  The manner in which a claim is
received,  examined  and  decided  is  itself  part  of  the
recognition the Scheme confers. A delayed, indifferent, or
hypertechnical process diminishes the honour, even where
2

--- Page 64 ---
the pension is eventually paid. 
3. Facts giving rise to the filing of this appeal in a
nutshell are that husband of the appellant, Late Shri
Ramakant Tripathi (the ‘deceased’) took part in  Maihar
State Praja Mandal Movement  of 1945-46 and was lodged in
Maihar Jail for 25 days. The claim of the deceased for
grant  of  Samman  Nidhi  under  the  Madhya  Pradesh
Swatantrata Sangram Sainik Sammannidhi Rules, 1972 (the
‘Rules’)  was  rejected  by  a  non-speaking  order  dated
06.04.1991 by the State Government.
4. The deceased passed away in 2016. After his death,
the appellant, on 29.02.2016, applied for grant of Samman
Nidhi. The aforesaid claim was rejected by an order dated
09.06.2016 by the Collector inter alia on the ground that
younger brother of the deceased and the villagers could
not provide any information with regard to deceased’s
role in the freedom movement and that the children of the
appellant were well placed and that she would receive
family pension.
5. The appellant, thereafter, sent a communication to
the Minister, General Administration Department, pursuant
to which an inquiry was conducted by the Collector, who
in his report dated 15.11.2016 affirmed the findings
3

--- Page 65 ---
recorded in the order dated 09.06.2016 and recommended
deletion of name of deceased from the freedom fighter’s
list maintained at the district level. 
6. On  07.12.2017,  the  appellant  submitted  a
representation to the Collector. The Tehsildar, in his
report dated 19.01.2018 recommended the grant of Samman
Nidhi to  the  appellant.  On  12.03.2019,  the  State
Government, while making a reference to the order dated
06.04.1991 which disallowed the claim of the deceased,
rejected the claim of the appellant holding that the
Rules do not provide for reconsideration. 
7. Being aggrieved, the appellant challenged the orders
dated 09.06.2016 and 12.03.2019 passed by the Collector
and the State Government respectively in a writ petition.
The learned Single Judge by an order dated 05.01.2023,
allowed the writ petition on the basis of an entry made
in Freedom Fighter’s List maintained by the Collector and
quashed the orders impugned therein. The learned Single
Judge further directed the State Government to grant
Samman Nidhi  to the appellant from 06.04.1991, that is
the date on which the claim of the deceased for grant of
Samman  Nidhi was rejected, along with interest at the
rate of 6% per annum. The State Government filed a review
4

--- Page 66 ---
petition  against  the  said  order,  which  came  to  be
dismissed on 15.10.2024.
8. The State Government, thereafter, preferred an appeal
before the Division Bench of the High Court. The Division
Bench by an order dated 14.02.2025, inter alia held that
deceased had accepted the order dated 06.04.1991 and did
not  challenge  the  same  during  his  lifetime.  It  was
further held that the claim of the appellant, made after
25 years was barred by delay, laches and estoppel. The
Division Bench relied on the findings of the Collector’s
Report dated 15.11.2016. It is in the aforesaid factual
background, the appellant has approached this Court.
9. We have heard learned counsel for the parties at
length and have perused the record.
10. The  object  of  the  Rules  is  to  honour  freedom
fighters. The Samman Nidhi  is, as its name suggests, a
mark of honour and is neither a bounty nor a dole. It is
an acknowledgment by the State of a debt which can never
be fully repaid. The freedom this country enjoys was
earned by the sacrifice of countless men and women, many
of whose names appear in no record. 
11.  This Court has held that object of grant of freedom
fighter’s pension is to honour freedom fighters and the
5

--- Page 67 ---
claim is not to be defeated merely because it was made
belatedly2. It is an equally well-settled proposition that
the  standard  of  proof  in  a  claim  seeking  freedom
fighter’s pension is not that of a criminal trial and the
claim has to be adjudicated on the basis of probabilities
and a claimant cannot be expected to produce documents of
events half a century old3. 
12. The claim of the appellant for grant of Samman Nidhi
is governed by the Rules. Rule 2(a) of the Rules which
defines the expression ‘family’ includes the wife as
well. Rule 2(b)(iii) of the Rules provides that ‘Freedom
Soldier’ means a person who had been imprisoned for one
day or more during the period between 1919 and 1946 in
connection with his political activities with the freedom
movement. Explanation 3 to Rule 2 of the Rules provides
that  where  any  person  is  unable  to  produce  a  jail
certificate in respect of his imprisonment or detention,
a  certificate  of  an  eminent  freedom  fighter  of  the
district  or  of  any  adjoining  district  shall  be
sufficient. Explanation 4 to Rule 2 of the Rules provides
2  Union of India v. Jai Kishun Singh, (2014) 10 SCC 352; State of Orissa v.
Choudhuri Nayak, (2010) 8 SCC 796; C. Venkat Reddy v. Union of India, (2009) 6
SCC 472; Union of India v. Avtar Singh, (2006) 6 SCC 493 and Mukund Lal Bhandari
v. Union of India, 1993 Supp (3) SCC 2
3  Kamlabai Sinkar v. State of Maharashtra, (2012) 11 SCC 754 and Gurdial
Singh v. Union of India, (2001) 8 SCC 8
6

--- Page 68 ---
where a soldier is unable to produce jail record/other
official proof, the certificate of an eminent freedom
fighter of the district or an adjoining district endorsed
by  the  present  or  former  member  of  Lok  Sabha  or
Legislative Assembly shall be accepted the individual
soldier being certified would need to have knowledge of
such soldier.
13. The  Nation’s  Obligation  to  Freedom  Fighters:  The
freedom  we  exercise  and  the  constitutional  institutions
through which we govern ourselves are the inheritance of a
struggle  sustained  by  ordinary  men  and  women.  Their
contribution cannot be measured by the prominence of their
names in public memory. In our view, the grant of Samman
Nidhi discharges  an  obligation  of  gratitude  that  has  its
source in the Constitution itself. That obligation is one of
recognition,  not  compensation.  It  is  owed  equally  to  the
known  and  the  unknown  participants  of  the  freedom
struggle, and it reaches the families who bore the cost of
their sacrifice. 
13.1 The  first  act  of  the  body  that  framed  our
Constitution  was  one  of  remembrance  for  the  freedom
struggle  and  the  debt  the  republic  owes  to  our  freedom
7

--- Page 69 ---
fighters. At midnight on 14 August 1947, as the Constituent
Assembly  assumed  power,  our  first  President  asked  the
members to  “recall in grateful remembrance the services
and  sacrifices  of  all  those  men  and  women,  known  and
unknown,  who  with  smiles  on  their  face  walked  to  the
gallows or faced bullets on their chests, who experience[d]
living death  in  the cells of the Andamans,  or spent long
years in the prisons of India”.4 The Assembly stood in silence
for  two  minutes,  and  each  member  took  a  pledge  which
began:  “At this solemn moment when the people of India,
through suffering and sacrifice, have secured freedom”.5 The
pledge credits freedom to “the people of India” , not to any
particular leader or party. It recalls that the price of that
freedom was “suffering and sacrifice” . And it treats service
to the nation as the proper response of those who inherited
what that sacrifice had secured. The framers acknowledged
this debt before a single provision of the Constitution was
adopted.
13.2 The  next  morning  our  first  Prime  Minister’s
message to the nation turned to  “the unknown volunteers
and soldiers of freedom who, without praise or reward, have
4  Constituent Assembly Debates, vol 5, 14 August 1947, 1 (Dr Rajendra 
Prasad)
5  ibid 9
8

--- Page 70 ---
served India even unto death”. 6 Many participants of the
Indian freedom struggle never reached a newspaper or a
history book. The Father of our Nation had called it the most
“genuinely democratic struggle for freedom”  in the history
of  the  world7.  The  struggle  was  one  that  reached  the
grassroots  of  the  nation  and  included  the  peasant  who
refused  to  pay  revenue,  the  student  who  left  college  to
mobilise the struggle, and the villager who sheltered those
in hiding. The nation’s gratitude must reach as far as the
struggle did. It belongs as much to the unnamed volunteer
as to those whose names every child learns.
13.3 This  gratitude  is  not  only  the  sentiment  of  the
founding generation. It is part of the constitutional order.
Article 51A(b) makes it the fundamental duty of every citizen
“to cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired our
national  struggle  for  freedom”.8 The  Swatantrata  Sainik
Samman Pension Scheme, 1980 was introduced to translate
this obligation into enduring public recognition and give this
obligation  an  institutional  status.  Originally  introduced  in
6  Jawaharlal Nehru, ‘The Appointed Day’ (15 August 1947) in S Gopal (ed), 
Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru, Second Series, vol 3 (Jawaharlal Nehru 
Memorial Fund 1985) 49.
7  MK Gandhi, ‘Speech at the AICC Meeting, Bombay’ (8 August 1942) in MK 
Gandhi, My Non-Violence (Navajivan Publishing House 1960) 183.
8  Constitution of India, art 51A(b), inserted by the Constitution (Forty-
second Amendment) Act 1976, s 11.
9

--- Page 71 ---
1972, the silver jubilee year of Independence, it became in
1980  a  ‘Samman’.  This  expression  conveys  it  all,  it  is
respect,  recognition  and  also  gratitude.  The  Samman
pension  is  payable  regardless  of  the  freedom  fighter’s
income.9 Its object is “to honour and where it was necessary,
also to mitigate the sufferings of those who had given their
all for the country ”.10 This Court noted that many freedom
fighters were reluctant to accept it at all, “as they would
consider  it  as  putting  a  price  on  their  patriotism”.11 The
pension is not simply compensation. It acknowledges a debt
that money cannot repay, but which must, for that reason,
not go unacknowledged. A nation is a community that spans
generations,  and  each  generation  that  enjoys  freedom
inherits the debt owed to those who secured it.
14. Supporting  Freedom  Fighters  and  Their  Families:  We
must now understand how this obligation of gratitude takes
its shape. Gratitude, unlike compensation, is not measured
by an account of what was lost. The cost of the sacrifice it
honours was borne not by the freedom fighter alone, but by
the family. And that sacrifice was made by men and women
9  Ministry of Home Affairs, Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme, 1980
(effective  1  August  1980)
https://www.mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2022-08/FFR_SwatantrataSainikSamma_200
32019%5B1%5D.pdf accessed 6 October 2026.
10  Mukund Lal Bhandari v Union of India 1993 Supp (3) SCC 2 [5].
11  State of Orissa v Choudhuri Nayak (2010) 8 SCC 796.
10

--- Page 72 ---
who  expected  nothing  in  return,  and  therefore  kept  no
account of it. Dr.  Rajendra Prasad spoke also of those, “who
not only lost wealth and property but cut themselves off
from near and dear ones”. 12 What the freedom fighter gave
was  not  only  time  in  prison.  It  was  the  life  they  would
otherwise have led. Lawyers gave up practice, bureaucrats
their  posts,  traders  their  shops.  The  household  lost  its
earning member, children their schooling, and elders their
care. The nation received the benefit, while it was often the
families who bore the cost. These sacrifices must translate
into  expressions  of  gratitude  and  continued
acknowledgement of debt owed to the families.
14.1 It is for this reason that the Scheme extends to
spouses and dependants, and to the families of martyrs. The
nation’s  response  mirrors  the  sacrifice  of  the  freedom
fighters; those who set aside their families for the country
are entitled to expect that the country will not set aside
their  families.  The  obligation  is  reciprocal  in  this  sense.
What was given to the nation at the cost of the family must,
to the extent it can be, be returned by the nation to the
family.
14.2 Nations  of  the  world  that  struggled  to  secure
12  Constituent Assembly Debates (n 1) 2.
11

--- Page 73 ---
freedom have recognised their obligations to the families of
the  freedom  fighters  in  a  similar  manner.  In  his  Second
Inaugural Address, Lincoln spoke of the nation’s duty “ to
care for him who shall have borne the battle, and for his
widow, and his orphan ”.13 The Supreme Court of the United
States has long held that laws for those who served must be
construed liberally, to protect those who were obliged “to
drop  their  own  affairs  to  take  up  the  burdens  of  the
nation”.14 South Africa’s Special Pensions Act, 1996 provides
for  those  whom  liberation  service  or  imprisonment
prevented from providing for their own retirement, and for
their survivors.15
14.3 The nature of the obligation also determines how
the Scheme must operate in practice. Because the pension
acknowledges  a  debt  owed  by  the  nation,  the  claimant
comes before the authority as one to whom something is
owed, not as a supplicant seeking a favour. The approach of
the authorities must therefore be practical, having regard to
the fact that most of the applications are by old persons
with no proper records. 16 And because the State, not the
13  Abraham Lincoln, ‘Second Inaugural Address’ (Washington DC, 4 March 1865).
14  Boone v Lightner 319 US 561, 575 (1943).
15  Special Pensions Act 69 of 1996 (South Africa), ss 1(1), 2–3.
16  Choudhuri Nayak (n 8) [8(iii)].
12

--- Page 74 ---
claimant, holds the jail registers, police files and gazettes of
the period, the burden of searching them falls on the State.
In Mukund Lal Bhandari , this Court went further, observing
that the Government “ should find out the freedom fighters
or their dependents and approach them with the pension
instead  of  requiring  them  to  make  applications”.17 The
manner in which a claim is received, examined and decided
is  itself  part  of  the  recognition  the  Scheme  confers.  A
delayed,  indifferent,  or  hypertechnical  process  diminishes
the honour, even where the pension is eventually paid.
14.4 The  generosity  with  which  the  Scheme  must  be
construed is, however, one side of the obligation. Gratitude
is meaningful only when it reaches those to whom it is owed.
Public faith in the obligation owed must not weaken.
15. In the backdrop of the aforesaid Rules, we turn to
the facts of the case in hand. The appellant has produced
certificates of Shri Shyamsundar Shyam, the then Member
of  Legislative  Assembly,  Dr.  Gaurishankar  Shastri,  a
former Legislator and President of State Freedom Fighters
Association who certified from their personal knowledge
that the deceased was in Maihar Jail for 25 days. The
17  Mukund Lal Bhandari (n 7) [4].
13

--- Page 75 ---
appellant had also produced a certificate issued by Shri
Surya  Pratap  Gautam,  the  Secretary  of  the  District
Freedom  Fighters’  Association  and  a  listed  freedom
fighter stating that deceased had worked with him in the
Praja  Mandal  Movement  and  a  certificate  by  Shri
Chintamani Shukla, another freedom fighter who saw the
deceased lodged in jail.
16. The fact that the deceased had participated in Praja
Mandal Movement is further fortified by the District
Freedom Fighters List maintained by the Collector. The
said record shows that deceased actively participated in
“Maihar  State  Prajamandal  Movement  1945-46”  and  was
lodged in jail in the year 1946.
17. The aforesaid material evidence on record has been
overlooked by the Division Bench. The plea of delay and
laches on which the claim of the appellant has been
negatived is equally untenable. The appellant is entitled
under  the  Rules  for  grant  of  Samman  Nidhi and  the
material on record indicates so. We are therefore unable
to sustain the order passed by the Division Bench.
14

--- Page 76 ---
18. For the foregoing reasons, the impugned order dated
14.02.2025 passed by the Division Bench is set aside and
the order dated 05.01.2023 passed by the learned Single
Judge is restored.
19. Having  regard  to  the  age  of  the  appellant,  the
respondents  shall  comply  with  the  direction  of  the
learned Single Judge within a period of four weeks.
20. For the reasons to follow, we have allowed the appeal
filed  by  Ms  Sushila  Tripathi,  wife  of  our  freedom
fighter.  Interlocutory  Application(s),  if  any,  shall
stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.13253-13254 OF 2026
(Arising out of S.L.P.(Civil) Nos.28406-28407 of 2024) 
INDORE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY   ... APPELLANT(S) 
                  VS.
AAYUSH GARG   ... RESPONDENT(S)
                                                         
          O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. These appeals call in question the correctness of
the judgment and orders dated 16th May, 2024 passed by the
High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Indore in Writ Petition
No. 4772 of 2023 and dated 21 st September, 2024 in Review
Petition No. 755 of 2024.  By the said judgment, the High
Court while allowing Interlocutory Application No.4023 of
2024 filed by the respondent in Writ Petition No.4772 of
2023, directed as under:
“31. Resultantly, without going into the merits
of the case, to maintain equity between the
parties, in the interest of justice and looking
to the limited relief sought by the petitioner
and as the petitioner was declared to be the
highest bidder in the said bid which is still
1

--- Page 94 ---
pending for its finalization, this petition s
disposed off with a direction that, Respondent
shall constitute a price fixation committee for
the subject plot no.7CB, Scheme No.140, Indore
and such committee shall determine the price
for  the  subject  plot  in  a  rational  and
pragmatic  manner  and  the  same  shall  be
communicated to the petitioner.  It is needless
to say that, price fixation committee should
adopt a proper legal mechanism and in any case,
foundation  for  determination  of  such  price
should be reasoned and logical, the same should
not be done in an arbitrary or biased manner.
32. This exercise shall be accomplished as
expeditiously as possible, within 4 weeks from
the date of communication of this order to
Respondent.
33. Once the price and schedule of payment are
communicated to the Petitioner, then petitioner
will, act upon the same within a period of 2
weeks from the date of communication made by
the Respondent and if the Petitioner accepts
the terms of the Respondent, then the allotment
letter of the subject plot will be issued to
the petitioner within 7 days from the date of
communication of acceptance made by petitioner.
34. However, it is made clear that, if the
schedule of payment is not complied with or
offer  is  not  accepted  by  petitioner,  then
Respondent would be at liberty to proceed ahead
in accordance of law, without reference to this
court.
2

--- Page 95 ---
35. This order has been passed in the peculiar
facts and circumstances of the case, which
cannot be treated as a precedent in any other
case.  With the aforesaid directions, the writ
petition and IA No.4023/2024 is disposed off.
No order as to costs.”
3. Brief  facts,  essential  for  disposal  of  these
appeals, are as follows:
(a) The  appellant,  on  07.09.2018,  issued
Advertisement No. 221 inviting bids for allotment of
various plots in Scheme No. 140 in the city of Indore,
Madhya  Pradesh.  In  furtherance  of  the  same,  the
respondent placed a bid for Plot No. 7-CB, situated in
Scheme No. 140. Along with the bid, the respondent also
furnished earnest money through a bank draft to the tune
of  Rs.  23,00,000/-  (Rupees  twenty  three  lakhs).  The
reserve price for Plot No. 7-CB was fixed at Rs. 69,000/-
(Rupees sixty nine thousand) per square meter, and the
respondent claims that he had offered a bid amount of Rs.
1,20,111/- (Rupees one lakh twenty thousand one hundred
eleven) per square meter. 
(b) Totally, seven bids were received, and the
respondent  turned out  to be  the highest  bidder. No
allotment letter had been issued, and the matter was
pending consideration with the appellant-Authority. The
3

--- Page 96 ---
advertisement itself was issued under a set of rules
called  the  Madhya  Pradesh  Vikas  Pradhikaran  Ki
Sampattiyon  Ka  Prabandhan  Tatha  Vyayan  Niyam,  2013
(hereinafter referred to as "the Rules").
(c) When matter stood thus, on an Interlocutory
Application at the instance of the land owners, whose
lands were acquired for the development of this Scheme
No. 140, in pending Writ Appeal No. 229 of 2008, a
Division Bench of the High Court directed to maintain
status  quo with  regard  to  the  suit  property  on
25.09.2018.
(d) It is not disputed that the appellant, apart from
taking steps to vacate the status quo, had also expressly
sought permission in the said Writ Appeal No. 229 of 2008
to proceed with the auction.
(e) At this stage, on 18 th August, 2022, the Division
Bench of the High Court disposed of Writ Appeal No. 229
of 2008 with the following operative order:
“24. Hence,  in  view  of  the  above
discussion,  the  writ  appeal  filed  by  Indore
Development  Authority  i.e.  WA  No.267/2008  is
dismissed.   The  writ  appeal  filed  by  the
petitioner society i.e. WA No.229/2008 is allowed
with the following direction/order/writ.
4

--- Page 97 ---
(i) Resolution No.199 dated 14.8.2007
and  order  dated  22.1.2008  are  hereby
quashed,
(ii) Resolution No.412 dated 3.10.2003
and agreement dated 7.11.2003 are hereby
restored,
(iii) The petitioner society is directed
to hand over the little documents and
possession on the spot of the entire land
of  area  2.121  hectares  to  the  Indore
Development Authority to make it a total
area of 10.25 hectares,
(iv) Subject  to  fulfilling  direction
no. (iii) the Indore Development Authority
shall allocate 20% of developed plots to
the petitioner society as per Resolution
No.412 dated 3.10.2003 and agreement dated
7.11.2003 within 90 days.
(v) If the petitioner society fails to
comply with direction No.(iii) within six
months  from  today  then  the  Indore
Development Authority shall be free from
the  agreement  dated  7.11.2003  and
Resolution No.199 dated 14.8.2007 and the
order dated 22.1.2008 shall be treated as
restored.
(vi) No order as to cost.”
It is not disputed that this judgment is pending in
several appeals filed before this Court.
5

--- Page 98 ---
(f) After  disposal  of  the  said  Writ  Appeal,  the
respondent filed Writ Petition No. 4772 of 2023 on 21 st
February, 2023 before the High Court, seeking a direction
to the appellant herein for issuance of an allotment
letter for Plot No. 7-CB in Scheme No. 140. 
(g) It  is,  at  this  stage,  the  matter  takes  an
interesting turn. The respondent, in the pending Writ
Petition, filed I.A. No. 4023 of 2024 praying for the
following relief:
“Therefore,  in  the  light  of  facts  and
circumstances of the case and in the interest
of natural justice, Hon’ble Court may kindly be
pleased  to  allow  this  application  and  the
present petition be disposed of with a limited
relief to the petitioner that, the subject plot
No.7CB, Scheme No.140, Indore be allotted to
the petitioner either by charging interest as
opined by the learned Advocate general or the
allotment of said plot be made on the rational
and pragmatic price fixed by price fixation
committee of IDA.”
4. It is in this Interlocutory Application that has
come to be allowed by the High Court by granting reliefs
which have been extracted hereinabove. 
5. Aggrieved,  the  appellant-authority,  after  having
lost the Review Petition also, has filed this appeal by
6

--- Page 99 ---
special leave. 
6. We heard Mr. Saurabh Mishra, learned senior counsel
for the appellant, and Mr. Devadatt Kamat, learned senior
counsel for the respondent and perused relevant material
placed on record.
7. Learned senior counsel for the appellant, drawing
attention to the Rules, contends that allotment can be
made only by a process of bid or by a process of lottery;
that the bids above Rs. 20,00,000/- (Rupees twenty lakhs)
under Rule 27 ought to be approved by the Board of the
Indore  Development  Authority;  that  under  the
advertisement,  the  Authority  has  right  to  accept  or
reject any bid; and that even the highest tenderer can be
awarded, only subject to the approval of the competent
authority. In this regard, learned senior counsel invited
attention to Clause 2 of the advertisement:
“2. Ordinarily the highest tenderer quoting
a rate higher than the reserve price shall be
declared as the selected tenderer, subject to
the approval of the competent authority on
opening of the tender envelopes.”
8. Inviting  attention  to  Rule  6(v)  of  the  Rules,
learned senior counsel contends that offers received
through  the  bids  are  to  be  opened  in  the  manner
7

--- Page 100 ---
prescribed in the relevant bid document and the rates
received shall be presented to the competent authority
under Rule 27 for a decision. Rule 6(v) further provides
that the competent authority ought to be satisfied that
there was sufficient competition or sufficient efforts
taken to obtain the best bid, and only after arriving at
such a satisfaction, approve the highest bid, if the
highest bid exceeds the reserve price. 
9. It is further contended that the Authority was
never at fault. 
10. In keeping the decision on allotment pending, as
the status quo order was operating, the appellant took
all steps bona fide to have the status quo order vacated
and the auction proceeded with.  Learned senior counsel
submits that today, much water has flown and eight years
have passed by since the date of the advertisement, and
great prejudice will be caused to public interest, if the
impugned order is given effect to. 
11. Learned senior counsel also submits that along with
the respondent, there were 97 other bidders who had also
submitted their bids. Learned senior counsel submits that
in those cases, a decision was taken to cancel the bids
and a fresh auction was ordered.   Learned senior counsel
8

--- Page 101 ---
fairly  points  out  that  the  decision  taken  for
cancellation and ordering of a fresh bid is the subject
matter of a writ petition in the High Court. 
12. Mr. Devadatt Kamat, learned senior counsel for the
respondent,  vehemently  defended  the  impugned  order.
Learned senior counsel submitted that the respondent was
admittedly the highest bidder and had offered an amount
in excess of 74% of the reserve price and three times the
circle  rate for  the said  property.  Learned senior
counsel submitted that ever since 2019, the respondent
has been pleading with the appellant for issuance of the
letter of allotment. Learned senior counsel submits that
the demands made by the respondent fell on the deaf ears
of the appellant. Learned senior counsel further submits
that even the status quo order was vacated on 18th August,
2022, and in spite of it, till the respondent moved the
Interlocutory Application in 2024, nothing was done.
According to learned senior counsel, the appellant had no
intention to take a decision. Learned senior counsel
contends  that  the  appellant  ought  to  have  taken  a
decision one way or the other and could not have left the
matter in limbo. 
13. Mr. Devadatt Kamat, learned senior counsel, also
contends that, in fact, the status quo order made on 25 th
9

--- Page 102 ---
September,  2018 did  not pertain  to the  property in
question.
14. In rejoinder, Mr. Saurabh Mishra, learned senior
counsel  for  the  appellant,  while  reiterating  the
submissions,  contended  that  the  appellant  had  filed
applications highlighting the aspect that the landowner
who had moved the Court in Writ Appeal No. 229 of 2008
had no concern with the land in question that is involved
in the present case. In fact, the appellant had pleaded
with the court to vacate the  status quo  and proceed.
Learned Counsel contends that the appellant was not at
fault as till the matter was disposed of on 18 th August,
2022, the status quo was not vacated.
15. We have considered the rival contentions.  We are
unable to sustain the impugned order. The direction of
the High Court directing the appellant to constitute a
Price  Fixation  Committee,  and  to  direct  that  such
committee "shall determine the price for the subject plot
in a rational and pragmatic manner", are all matters
totally beyond the ken of the governing Rules. 
16. Moreover,  at  the  stage  when  the  respondent
approached  the  High  Court,  the  respondent  had  no
indefeasible right to allotment and no vested rights had
10

--- Page 103 ---
been crystallized in favor of the respondent warranting
the issue of any mandamus in their favour. 
17. As is clear from the Rules discussed above, the
ultimate decision to award the tender or not was to vest
with the competent authority, which was to decide under
Rule 6(v) read with Rule 27 whereunder the decision was
to be approved by the Board.  Before the appellant could
resort  to  any  of  these  procedural  requirements,  the
respondent had moved the Writ Petition and in the Writ
Petition moved an Interlocutory Application pressing for
a limited relief which the High Court had gone on to
grant.
18. Under the circumstances, we set aside the orders
dated 16th May, 2024 passed by the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh at Indore in Writ Petition No. 4772 of 2023 and
dated 21st September, 2024 in Review Petition No. 755 of
2024.  
19. At  this  stage,  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
respondent submitted that the main Writ Petition should
be remanded to the High Court for a decision on the other
aspects of the matter.
20. We did consider the feasibility of that option.
11

--- Page 104 ---
21. However, we are not inclined to remand the Writ
Petition, as it will be a futile exercise.  The appellant
has to first take a decision on what it proposes to do
with  the  bids  that  have  been  received  in  question
pursuant to advertisement No.221 issued on 7 th September,
2018 and, more particularly, with regard to plot No.7-CB
in Scheme No.140.
22. Hence, the appropriate course of action would be to
direct the appellant to decide on the course of action
that it proposes to take on the bids received with regard
to plot No.7-CB in Scheme No.140 within a period of four
weeks from the date of receipt of this order.  Any
decision taken shall be communicated to the respondent.
The respondent, if aggrieved, will be at liberty to
pursue such remedies as are available to him in law and
if those remedies are resorted to, they will be decided
on their own merits.
23. Learned senior counsel for the respondent, at this
stage, submits that already a representation dated 30 th
December, 2022 made by the respondent is pending with the
appellant.   The  appellant  shall  consider  the  said
representation and take a decision in accordance with
law.
12

--- Page 105 ---
24. The appeals are accordingly disposed of in the
above terms.  There shall be no order as to costs.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We are in the midst of hearing the civil appeals/special leave petitions.
Hearing stands adjourned for the day for the purpose indicated hereinbelow. 
2. The teachers represented by Ms. Aparna Bhat, learned senior counsel,
numbering  a few thousand were appointed  between 1991 and 2000.  Since

--- Page 119 ---
13
furnishing details of all these teachers would be a humungous exercise, we
require information in respect of any one teacher, appointed in each of the 10
(ten) years between 1991 and 2000, in respect of the following points:
i. The advertisement in response to which the teacher applied
for  recruitment  and  the  qualifications  required  (copy  of  the
advertisement may be enclosed, if available);
ii. Name of the College and the University to which such college
is affiliated; 
iii. Qualification  possessed  by  the  teacher  as  mentioned  by
him/her at the time applying for the post of teacher;
iv.   Subject for which the application was submitted by the teacher;
v.    Date of appointment / regularisation;
vi.   Date of acquiring NET / SET by such teacher;
vii.  Date of acquiring M. Phil / Ph. D by such teacher, if any; 
viii.  Date  of  exemption  granted  by  the  UGC  in  respect  of  such
teacher;
3. These particulars may be furnished on affidavit. 
4. Selection of the teachers is left to the discretion of Ms.  Bhat.
5. Re-list the appeals and special leave petitions on 3 rd November, 2026
after fresh matters. 
(JATINDER KAUR)                             (SUDHIR KUMAR SHARMA)
P.S. to REGISTRAR                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No. 1888 OF 2011
SURINDER ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF HARYANA ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. Appellant was convicted under Section 302 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’)  by the learned
Additional Sessions Judge, Rohtak  vide  the judgment and
order dated 01.08.2000 passed in Sessions Case No.97 of
1998 and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life.
3. Appeal filed by the appellant before the High Court
of Punjab and Haryana (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter)
in Criminal Appeal No.369 DB of 2000 came to dismissed
vide the impugned judgment and order dated 04.11.2019.
1

--- Page 133 ---
4. This  Court  vide  order  dated  21.01.2011  had
issued notice on the application for condonation of delay as
well as on the Special Leave Petition. Thereafter,  vide  the
order dated 30.09.2011, delay was condoned and leave was
granted. Considering the fact that appellant was in custody
at that point of time for more than 9 years, appellant was
released on bail.
5. In the hearing held on 14.07.2026, the following
order came to be passed:
1. Ms. Pearl Pundir, learned counsel submits that
her Senior was  appointed  as  legal  aid  counsel  to
represent  the  appellant  in  this  Criminal  Appeal.
However, recently he has tendered his resignation. 
2. This is an old pending matter. 
3. We,  therefore,  appoint Mr.  Mohammad  Aslam,
learned counsel who is present in the Court, as an
Amicus Curiae to assist the Court. 
4. We request learned counsel for the respondent-
State of Haryana to furnish a soft copy of the case
record to the learned Amicus Curiae.
5. At this stage, learned counsel for the respondent-
State of Haryana submits that many portions of the
soft copy of the case record are not legible. 
6. We,  therefore,  permit  learned  counsel  for  the
parties to approach the Registry for obtaining legible
hard copies of the case record.
2

--- Page 134 ---
6. As per the prosecution, the complainant and his
three brothers were residing at Babra Mohalla near Sadar
Police Station, Rohtak. On 04.04.1998, one Kamlesh came
to the house of the complainant around 07:00-08:00 am in
the  morning  for  delivery  of  milk.  Kamlesh  informed  the
complainant  that  his  elder  brother  Raju  did  not  make
payment for the milk purchased. She gave an ultimatum to
the  complainant  that  by  evening  Raju  should  make  the
payment. In the evening Raju told the complainant that he
was going to the house of the appellant Surinder (husband
of Kamlesh) for making the payment. At around 10:00 pm,
one Mukesh, PW-12, informed the complainant that Raju
was murdered by Surinder and his wife Kamlesh with a
Gandasa.
7. Based on  this, FIR No.233 of 1998 was lodged
before  the  Police  Station  Sadar,  Rohtak  under  Sections
302/34 IPC.
8. After completion of investigation, charge-sheet was
submitted, whereafter the case was committed to the Court
of  the  Additional  Sessions  Judge.  Both  Surinder  and
Kamlesh pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.
3

--- Page 135 ---
9. The prosecution examined 15 witnesses to prove its
case.  At  the  conclusion  of  the  prosecution  evidence,  the
statements of Surinder and Kamlesh were recorded under
Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.PC).
Thereafter, the learned Additional Sessions Judge convicted
and sentenced the appellant as above, while acquitting his
wife, Kamlesh, of the charges so framed against her.
10. As noticed supra, the conviction and sentence of
the appellant was affirmed by the High Court.
11. Learned amicus submits that the prosecution case
is based on the sole testimony of PW-12 Mukesh, who was
projected as the eyewitness. However, the testimony of PW-12
cannot be believed at all. Apart from that, he submits that
the  forensic  examination  of  the  bloodstains  found  on  the
seized clothes of the appellant and on the Gandasa did not
match  with  the  bloodstains  of  the  deceased.  In  such
circumstances,  the  trial  court  erred  in  convicting  the
appellant as above. The High Court committed a manifest
error in affirming such conviction and sentence.
12. On  the  other  hand,  learned  State  counsel  has
4

--- Page 136 ---
defended  the  impugned  conviction  and  sentence  of  the
appellant by the trial court, as affirmed by the High Court.
He submits from the compilation prepared by him, that the
clothes and the Gandasa were recovered on the basis of the
disclosure statement of the appellant made under Section
27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. He further submits
that  it is quite but natural  that  there would be certain
degree of inconsistency in the evidence of the prosecution
witnesses  but  that  would  not  be  fatal  to  prove  the
prosecution case. If the testimony of PW-12 is considered as
a whole and together with the testimony of Dr. S.S. Dahiya-
PW-5, it would be apparent that the death of Raju was
homicidal  and  was  caused  because  of  the  fatal  injuries
suffered by him at the hands of the appellant. No other view
is possible.
13. Submissions  made  by  learned  counsel  for  the
parties have received the due consideration of the Court.
14. Since  heavy  reliance  has  been  placed  on  the
testimony  of PW-12, it would be apposite to refer to and
examine the said evidence at the outset. In his examination-
in-chief,  PW-12  stated  that  at  around  9:30  p.m.  on
5

--- Page 137 ---
04.04.1998, as he had reached the house of one Babal, he
heard the noise of ‘mar diya, mar diya’ from the house of
the appellant, Surinder. He stated that he had gone to the
house of the appellant and saw him giving a blow on the
head of Raju with the Gandasa. He also saw Kamlesh giving
Gandasa blow on the fingers of Raju. According to him,
Raju  succumbed  to  his  injuries  in  the  house  of  the
appellant itself. It was thereafter that he went to the house
of  the  deceased  and  narrated  the  entire  episode  to  the
complainant.
15. However, in his cross-examination, he stated that
he did not enter the house of the appellant and had seen
the occurrence from outside the main gate. The door of the
house of the appellant was closed, but it was not bolted.
Though he stated that the appellant had inflicted blows on
the deceased in his presence, he contradicted himself by
saying that he did not enter into the house of the appellant
to  intervene  or  to  save  Raju  from  the  clutches  of  the
appellant and Kamlesh. He also did not raise any noise
though he was standing on the street outside the house of
the appellant.
6

--- Page 138 ---
16. Thus, from the evidence of PW-12 itself, it is quite
clear  that  there  are  vital  material  contradictions  in  his
deposition. While in his examination-in-chief he stated that
he had seen the appellant inflict a  Gandasa blow on the
deceased, but in his cross-examination, he stated that he
was standing on the street outside the main gate of the
house of the appellant which was closed; even the door of
the house of the appellant was closed. Question is, if the
door of the house of the appellant was closed, how could he
have witnessed the incident of the appellant and Kamlesh
giving  blows  to  the  deceased  by  Gandasa?  In  such
circumstances, it would not be safe at all to place reliance
on  the  testimony  of  PW-12,  as  it  cannot  be  said  to  be
trustworthy.
17. That  brings  us  to  the  report  of  the  Forensic
Science Laboratory. As per the Forensic Science Laboratory
report (Exhibit P-Z), the bloodstains found on the seized
clothes of the appellant were found to be of human origin;
however, no conclusive opinion could be rendered regarding
the blood group.  Even the serological examination of the
deceased was also found to be inconclusive.
7

--- Page 139 ---
18. To hold that the examined samples were of human
blood is one thing, but to get it matched with the blood
sample of the deceased is another thing. Unless the blood
samples  found  on  the  seized  clothes  of  the  appellant
matches  with  the  blood  sample  of  the  deceased,  no
definitive conclusion can be reached about the involvement
of the appellant in the murder of the deceased. That apart,
even the serological analysis of the bloodstains found on
the  Gandasa was  incomplete  as  the  material  had
disintegrated.
19. No doubt, the deceased had met an unfortunate
end.  However,  the  question  is  whether  the  evidence  on
record  is  sufficient  to  hold  the  appellant  guilty  of
committing  the homicidal death  of  the deceased. In our
opinion,  it  cannot  be  said  that  prosecution  had  proved
beyond all reasonable doubt that it was the appellant, and
only  the  appellant,  who  had  caused  the  death  of  the
deceased. There is nothing on record to link the appellant
with  the  homicidal  death  of  the  deceased.  This  view  is
reinforced  by  the  acquittal  of  Kamlesh.  In  such
circumstances, the benefit of doubt would have to be given
8

--- Page 140 ---
to the appellant.
20. Both  the  trial  court  as  well  as the  High Court
erred in convicting the appellant under Section 302 IPC.
21. Consequently,  the  judgment  and  order  of  the
learned Additional Sessions Judge dated 01.08.2000 and
that of the High Court dated 04.11.2019 are hereby set
aside.
22. The  appellant  is  acquitted  of  the  charge  under
Section 302 IPC.
23. The bail bonds stands discharged.
24. The appeal is allowed.
25. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed
of.

(UJJAL BHUYAN)
......................J.

WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.524/2024 
O R D E R
Diary Nos. 58089/2024 and  58123/2024
The instant Special Leave Petitions have been preferred by the
petitioner,  challenging  the  orders  dated  24.09.2019  passed  by  the
learned Single Judge of the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan,
Bench at Jaipur, in S.B. Criminal Appeal No. 1134 of 2019 and S.B.
Criminal Appeal No. 1135 of 2019. Moreover, arising from the common
set of facts as involved in the aforementioned Special Leave Petitions,
is   a  writ  petition  bearing  W.P.(Crl)  No. 524  of 2024,  filed  by  the
1

--- Page 144 ---
 petitioner before this Court, seeking the following reliefs:
“a) Issue a writ in the nature of certiorari or any other
appropriate  writ,  order  or  direction,  setting  aside  the
enquiry proceedings initiated against the Petitioner under
Rule 16 of the Rajasthan Civil Services (Classification,
Control  and  Appeal)  Rules,  1958  on  the  basis  of  the
adverse remark/observation made in the judgments and
orders  dated  24.09  2019  passed  by  the  Hon'ble  High
Court of Rajasthan at Jaipur in S.B Criminal Appeal No.
1134/2019 and S.B Criminal Appeal No. 1135/2019; and
b) Pass such other order or orders as this Hon'ble Court
may deem fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of
the case.”
2. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that the petitioner herein,
at the relevant time, was posted as Special Judge, meant for Protection
of Children from Sexual Offences Act and Commission for Protection of
Child Rights Act, (POCSO Act) Dholpur, Rajasthan. In a criminal case
arising out of FIR No. 557 of 2016, the petitioner/judicial officer, by a
common order dated 04.05.2019, had granted bail to two accused
persons, namely Punjab Singh and Aishveer Singh. Challenging the
grant of bail, the complainant had preferred S.B. Criminal Appeal No.
1134 of 2019 and S.B. Criminal Appeal No. 1135 of 2019 before the
High Court.
2

--- Page 145 ---
3. The learned Single Judge of the High Court, by orders dated
24.09.2019, allowed both the appeals, set aside the common order
dated  04.05.2019  and  cancelled  the  bail  granted  to  said  accused
persons on the ground that no change of circumstance had occurred
after the appeals and revision petitions of the accused persons against
the  rejection  of  their  earlier  bail  applications  were  dismissed.  The
relevant paragraphs of the impugned order dated 24.09.2019 passed
in S.B. Criminal Appeal No. 1134 of 2019, are extracted as under:
“16.  In  my  considered  view,  in  the  present  matter  no
change in the circumstances took place after the revision
seeking bail was dismissed by Coordinate Bench of this
Court. I am of the considered view that the learned trial
court has committed gross illegality in granting bail to the
accused, more particularly when the revision seeking bail
was dismissed by the Coordinate Bench of this Court after
considering statement of the victim and looking to the
seriousness of the offence, the reason assigned by the
learned trial court that the accused is in custody since
18-4-2017, in my considered view may not be a relevant
consideration  for  exercising  discretion  in  favour  of  the
accused under Section 439 Cr.P.C., as has been held by
the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the matter of  Anil Kumar
Yadav (supra).
 
17. Thus, in the facts and circumstances of this case the
Registry is directed to place a copy of this order before the
Hon’ble Chief Justice for information.
3

--- Page 146 ---
 
18. In that view of the matter, the present application for
cancellation of bail is allowed. The order passed by the
learned trial court dated 4-5-2019 is set aside. The bail
bonds of the accused are directed to be cancelled and the
learned Trial Judge is directed to take the accused into
custody and proceed with the trial of the case.”
4. Pursuant  to  the  order  of  the  learned  Single  Judge,  the  High
Court issued a Statement of Memorandum dated 25.10.2024, along
with  the  chargesheet,  proposing  to  hold  an  inquiry  against  the
petitioner/judicial  officer  under  Rule  16  of  the  Rajasthan  Civil
Services  (Classification,  Control  and  Appeal)  Rules,  1958  on  the
charge that the act of the petitioner in allowing the bail applications of
the aforementioned two accused persons amounted to gross judicial
impropriety and indiscipline.
5. Aggrieved by the remarks made by the learned Single Judge in
the impugned orders as well as the inquiry proceedings initiated by
the High Court, the petitioner is before this Court. In the Writ Petition
filed by the petitioner, the aforesaid prayers have been made.
4

--- Page 147 ---
6. We have heard Shri P.S Patwalia, learned senior counsel for the
petitioner,   Shri  Raju  Ramachandran,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing  for  the  High  Court  and  learned  counsel  Sri.  S.  Udaya
Kumar Sagar for the State and  perused the material on record.
7. The genesis of this controversy emanates from paragraphs 16
and 17 of the order dated 24.09.2019 passed in S.B.Criminal Appeal
No.1134/2019 which are extracted above. The learned Single Judge of
the  High  Court  who  passed  the  said  order  had  stated  that  the
petitioner herein was not right in granting the relief of bail to the
accused. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, the
Registry of the High Court was directed to place a copy of the said
order before the Hon’ble Chief Justice of the High  Court  for
information. 
8. When the Hon’ble Chief Justice of the High Court was made
aware of the said order, the Memorandum dated 25.10.2024 along
with  statement  of  charges  under  Rule  16  of  the  Rajasthan  Civil
Services  (Classification,  Control  and  Appeal)  Rules,  1958  and  the
allegation of charge were issued to the petitioner herein.
5

--- Page 148 ---
9. Assailing  the  same, Writ Petition  (Criminal)  No.524/2024 has
been  filed.   As  noted  above,  concomitantly,  the  petitioner/judicial
officer has also assailed the order dated 24.09.2019 passed by the
learned Single Judge in S.B.Criminal Appeal No.1134/2019.
10. We  find  that having regard to the facts and  circumstances of
this case, the observations of the learned Single Judge in order dated
24.09.2019 passed in S.B.Criminal Appeal No.1134/2019 would not
call  for  any  modification  or  expunction.  In  the  circumstances,  we
dismiss these Special Leave Petitions. 
11.  However, the question is, whether, the Hon’ble Chief Justice of
the High Court could have initiated disciplinary proceedings against
the petitioner herein.  The Hon’ble  Chief  Justice  had  many
avenues by which the case of the  petitioner/judicial  officer  could
have been remedied. The petitioner/judicial officer could have been
summoned and impressed as well as warned upon the manner in
which he had disposed  of  the  subsequent  bail  application  when
earlier a similar application had been rejected by the High Court.  In
6

--- Page 149 ---
other words, the earlier order of the High Court could have been borne
in mind and given its due weightage and seriousness by the petitioner
– Judicial Officer when the subsequent application for bail was filed by
the accused. The same not having emanated from the impugned order
passed by the petitioner/judicial officer when the relief of bail was
granted by the petitioner herein to the accused has possibly led to the
learned Single Judge making remarks in paragraphs 16 and 17 of his
order.
12. However, the Hon’ble Chief Justice of the High Court sought to
initiate  an  inquiry  into  the  matter.  We  find  that  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of this case, the initiation of an inquiry was not at all
required. Possibly the entry of the remarks of the learned Single Judge
in the Annual Confidential Report (ACR) would have sufficed. We have
also stated, the petitioner/judicial officer could have been counseled
and  warned  to  be  more  careful  in  future  and  to  give  sufficient
weightage to the orders of the High Court particularly when the same
were  passed  earlier  in  the  same  case  by  the  High  Court.  In  the
circumstance,  we  find  that  the  Memorandum  dated 25.10.2024 at
Annexure P-6, the statement of charges under Rule 16 of the Rules,
the allegation of charge etc. were not warranted for in the instant case.
13. We also note that the ACR pertaining to the petitioner has been
7

--- Page 150 ---
positive and he is shown to  have  been  a  very  good  officer.  The
petitioner herein has since retired on 31.03.2026 on attaining the age
of superannuation.  His pay as per the revised pay scale and terminal
benefits have not been released although his provisional pension may
have been sanctioned and released.
14. In  the  circumstances,  we  deem  it  just  and  proper  to  quash
Memorandum dated 25.10.2024 at Annexure  P-6,  the  statement  of
charges  under  Rule  16  of  the  Rules,  the  allegation  of  charge  etc.
Consequently, we direct the respondent(s)/State and High Court to
take  steps  to  re-compute  the  pay  as  per  revised  pay  scale  of  the
petitioner/judicial officer and release his terminal benefits including
pension  and  arrears  of  pension  and  pay  within  a  period  of  three
months if there is no other legal impediment to do so.
15. We  clarify  that  the  aforesaid  discussion  and  order  is  passed
having regard to the peculiar facts of this case. 
16. All  Pending applications  including  the  applications  for
condonation of delay shall stand disposed of.
As noted above, Special Leave Petitions stand dismissed.
8

--- Page 151 ---
W.P.(Crl.) No. 524/2024
17. In view of the aforesaid order, the Writ Petition is allowed.
Pending application(s) shall stand disposed of.

                   M/S. Brajesh Pandey & Associates, AOR
                   Mr. Brajesh Pandey, Adv.
                   Ms. Divya Negi, Adv.
                   Mr. Ankit Ranjan Pandey, Adv.
                   
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Intervention applications/Impleadment are allowed.
2. Delay condoned. 
3. The petitioners herein had applied for appointment on the
post  of  Intermediate  Trained  Teachers  under  the  Para
Teacher Category. 50 per cent of the posts were reserved
for the para teacher category whereas the remaining were
for non-para teacher category. In the non-para teacher
category, there was no benefit of age relaxation though,
essential eligibility qualifications were same for both
categories. However, in the para teacher category, there
was benefit of age relaxation available.
4. In Pawan Singh Choudhary & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand
2

--- Page 156 ---
& Ors.1, another matter which came before a Division Bench
of the High Court, the issue that arose for consideration
was whether candidates who had applied under the para
teacher category and were otherwise qualified, including
age-wise, for appointment in the non-para teacher category,
could be considered for appointment on the posts earmarked
for  non-para  teacher  category.  In  that  context,  the
Division Bench of the High Court opined that there is no
requirement for such applicants i.e., those who applied
under  para  teacher  category  to  separately  apply  for
appointment  on  posts  earmarked  for  non-para  teacher
category, if otherwise they are eligible, including age-
wise, and have been placed higher in the order of merit
than the last selected candidate in the non-para teacher
category.
5. The same issue arose in a bunch of writ petition(s) before
the learned Single Judge of the High Court wherein the
grievance of the candidates was that though they have
secured marks higher than the last selected candidate in
the  non-para  teacher  category,  they  were  not  being
considered for appointment against posts earmarked for non-
para teacher category because they had applied under para
teacher category. The learned Single Judge disposed of the
writ petition(s) by requiring the State-respondent to hold
one  last  consolidated  counseling  for  all  categories.
1  LPA No. 186/2017
3

--- Page 157 ---
Besides, the learned Single Judge clarified that the issue
whether candidates applying under the para teacher category
were eligible for consideration against non-para teacher
category posts, if they meet the age bar, has already been
decided by a Division Bench of the High Court in  Pawan
Singh Choudhary case.
6. The State preferred an intra-court appeal against the order
of the learned Single Judge of the High Court. By the
impugned order, the Division Bench of the High Court upheld
the order passed by the learned Single Judge and issued a
slew of directions.
7. As there was no specific direction declaring candidates
applying  under  the  para  teacher  category  eligible  for
consideration against posts earmarked for non-para teacher
category, the petitioners have filed these Special Leave
Petitions.
8. We have considered the submissions made before us and have
perused the orders of the learned Single Judge as well as
the Division Bench of the High Court. The Division Bench
has not issued any direction at variance with the earlier
view of the High Court that a candidate who had applied
under the para teacher category could be considered against
the posts earmarked for non-para teacher category provided
he holds the requisite qualification and falls within the
4

--- Page 158 ---
age limit. In such circumstances, the earlier decision
enabling  a  candidate  applying  under  the  para  teacher
category to be considered against posts earmarked for the
non-para teacher category, if he is otherwise qualified and
meets the age bar by the last date of submission of the
application, is still effective and applicable. 
9. In such circumstances, we are of the view that the orders
passed by the learned Single Judge as well as by the
Division Bench of the High Court do not call for any
modification or clarification. In case those orders are not
being complied with, it is always open to the petitioners
to take recourse to the contempt jurisdiction of the High
Court.
10. With the aforesaid observations and liberty, the special
leave petitions and all pending applications stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.       OF 2026
(@ SLP(CRL.) No. 13532/2026)
DIRECTORATE OF ENFORCEMENT                          APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
BHUPESH ARORA                                      RESPONDENT(S)
 
WITH
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.       OF 2026
(@ SLP(Crl) No. 16623/2026)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We  have  heard  the  learned  Additional  Solicitor  General
appearing for the Directorate of Enforcement and the learned
senior counsel appearing for the respective accused persons. 
3. SLP(CRL.) No. 13532/2026 has been filed by the appellant –
Directorate of Enforcement against the bail granted by the

--- Page 176 ---
2
High Court to the respondent – Bhupesh Arora vide order dated
23.02.2026 and SLP(CRL.) No.  16623/2026 has been filed by the
appellant/accused  –  Rohit  Vij  seeking  grant  of  bail  in
connection with ECIR/HYZO/46/2022 dated 14.10.2022 under the
provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
(for short, the ‘PMLA’).
4. The sum and substance of the prosecution's case qua the
respondent – Bhupesh Arora in  SLP(CRL.) No. 13532/2026 and
the appellant – Rohit Vij in  SLP(CRL.) No.16623/2026 is as
under:-
“First, The public invested in the 'LOXAM' app
in the belief that it belonged to a French
multinational. Their money reached a virtual
account held by M/s Xindai Technologies Pvt.
Ltd.
Second, Xindai spread the money across its 29
virtual  accounts.  Three  parallel  shells,
namely Betench, Xitamin and Skhalita, did the
same with their collections. From there the
money passed into 38 physical accounts (which
also  included  the  IndusInd  Bank  operated
directly by Sh. Bhupesh Arora) and then into
about 35 mule accounts.
Third, the mule accounts remitted the money by
RTGS to M/s Ranjan Moneycorp Pvt. Ltd. and M/s
KDS Forex Pvt. Ltd. These two are the only

--- Page 177 ---
3
RBI-licensed entities in the chain, and the
licence is what let the tainted money enter a
regulated channel [Note: this was the stage at
which Rohit Vij had facilitated the layering
of the POC]. The funds were further layered
through the other shell entities which were
controlled by Sh. Bhupesh Arora.
Fourth, Sh. Rohit Vij turned the RTGS credits
into Dollars and Dirhams by buying currency
from other money changers. He kept 0.3 to 0.7
per cent as commission, and his two companies
withdrew about Rs. 75 crore in cash. Once the
money became foreign currency in cash, the
trail ended.
Fifth, the petitioner handed the currency to
Sahil Bajaj, Pankaj Wadhwa and Anurag Aggarwal
against a token, namely the serial number of a
currency note. They carried it to Dubai and
China  through  hawala  operators  and
cryptocurrency.
In short, the victim's money entered the chain
as a bank credit and left the country as cash
dollars.”
5. Placing reliance upon the aforesaid, the learned Additional
Solicitor General appearing for the Directorate of Enforcement
firstly submits that both the accused persons are a flight
risk. The accused – Bhupesh Arora is the mastermind and in

--- Page 178 ---
4
control of the said entities, with the same IP being used for
all the companies. The role of the accused – Rohit Vij comes
thereafter. Apart from the huge sum of transactions involved,
as indicated in the scheme of layering, it is a case of money
being  transferred  out  of  the  country  to  various  other
countries. 
6. It is further submitted that the High Court has committed an
error in placing reliance on the quashing of a single FIR,
that too on a compromise, and, thereafter, holding that the
accused - Bhupesh Arora cannot be proceeded with in the
predicate offence. It is also submitted that the High Court
was right in declining the bail insofar as the accused – Rohit
Vij is concerned, particularly, when the investigation is not
completed, and the proceeds of crime involved might be much
more than the amount indicated in the prosecution complaint
totaling to more than Rs.2000 crores. It is reiterated that
the conduct of both the accused persons does not facilitate
granting them bail, as they are a flight risk and, in fact,
have made attempts to flee the country.
7. Learned Senior counsel appearing for the accused – Bhupesh
Arora and the accused – Rohit Vij would submit that there is
no specific material to implicate them. The Red Corner Notice
issued against accused - Bhupesh Arora has been quashed. In
the predicate offence also, accused - Bhupesh Arora was not

--- Page 179 ---
5
made an accused. Inasmuch as the prosecution complaint has
already been filed, there is no need for any interference with
the impugned order granting bail to accused – Bhupesh Arora in
SLP(Crl.) No.13532/2026. 
8. Insofar as accused - Rohit Vij is concerned, it is submitted
that he has been under incarceration for about 15 months. And,
in view of the more serious role allegedly played by accused –
Bhupesh Arora, who has already been granted bail by the High
Court, SLP(Crl.) No.16623/2026 filed by accused - Rohit Vij
seeking bail ought to be allowed by setting aside the impugned
judgment.
9. Having heard the learned ASG and the learned Senior Counsel
appearing for the respective parties, the following are our
findings. 
10. The predicate offence has been quashed on a compromise, which
factum is not in dispute. There are numerous other FIRs that
have been filed. What is relevant is the existence of proceeds
of crime. In our considered view, the High Court in SLP(Crl.)
No.13532/2026 was not correct in dealing with the factual
issues, apart from taking note of the FIR(s) quashed by
compromise. Mere quashing of an FIR, by a compromise per se,
will not obliterate the existence of the proceeds of crime. In
other words, the Court must be concerned only with the crime
that creates proceeds for the subsequent action of money

--- Page 180 ---
6
laundering that is punishable under the mandate of the PMLA. 
11. Having gone through the allegations made, which are quite
serious,  we  are  of  the  considered  view  that  further
investigation is certainly required, as the extent of money
laundering is likely to span across the country. The amount
stated to be involved is also very huge. Suffice it to state
that the High Court ought not to have granted bail to accused
–  Bhupesh  Arora,  taking  note  of  the  facts  governing,
especially when the said accused has entered the country
during the currency of a Red Corner Notice which is stated to
have been quashed on a technical plea. Hence, we are inclined
to set aside the bail granted to accused – Bhupesh Arora.
12. We are also not inclined to grant bail to the appellant –
Rohit Vij in SLP(Crl.) No.16623/2026, especially when the
investigation has not yet been completed, and the nature of
allegations do not warrant the grant of bail. Certainly, the
rigour of Section 45 of the PMLA has to be pressed into
service for both the accused persons. 
13. Thus, taking into consideration the facts governing, we set
aside the impugned order in SLP(Crl.) No.13532/2026 and uphold
the impugned order in SLP(Crl.) No.16623/2026. However, by
taking note of the submissions made, on instructions, by the
learned ASG, we expect the investigation to be completed by
the Directorate of Enforcement within a period of five months

--- Page 181 ---
7
from the date of receipt of a copy of this order. Thereafter,
liberty is given to the respondent/accused – Bhupesh Arora in
SLP(Crl.) No.13532/2026 and appellant/accused – Rohit Vij in
SLP(Crl.) No.16623/2026 to file a fresh bail application
before the concerned Special Court seeking regular bail, in
which case, the impugned order and the order passed by this
Court will not stand in their way. 
14. The  respondent/accused  –  Bhupesh  Arora  in  SLP(Crl.)
No.13532/2026 is granted two weeks time to surrender from the
date of receipt of a copy of this order. 
15. The accused - Bhupesh Arora shall show his current location at
all times to the Directorate of Enforcement, and we make it
clear that he is not to be arrested till the expiry of the
time granted for his surrender. Additionally, a condition is
imposed on him to the effect that he shall not leave the
country till the expiry of the time granted for his surrender.
16. In such view of the matter, the appeal arising out of
SLP(Crl.) No.13532/2026 stands allowed and the appeal arising
out of SLP(Crl.) No.16623/2026 stands dismissed.

--- Page 182 ---
8
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

2026 INSC 1123
1
    (REPORTABLE ORDER) 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
    CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal  No(s).  8092/2013
ISLAM HUSSAIN & ORS.                             Appellant(s)
                             VERSUS
HAJARI LAL & ANR.                                Respondent(s)
      O R D E R
1. This appeal arises out of the
order passed by the High Court of Judicature
at Allahabad on 11.09.2012 in Civil Misc Writ
Petition  No  12738/2004  dismissing  the
appellants’ Writ Petition which, in turn, was
preferred against the order dated 04.03.1998
passed by the Additional Judge, Small Cause
Court, Varanasi dismissing appellants’ suit
for ejectment and recovery of arrears of rent
as also the revisional order dated 17.12.2003
of  Additional  District  Judge,  Court  No.1,
Varanasi,  dismissing  appellants’  J.S.C.C.
Revision No. 22 of 1998.
2. Considering the nature of order
we propose to pass, we are not dwelling on
every minute details of the lis between the

--- Page 195 ---
2
parties. Suffice it would be to mention that
the appellants inducted the respondent no.1 as
tenant in two shops (hereinafter referred to
as the "shop A” and "shop B") , however, the
respondent no.1,  Hajari Lal , entered into a
partnership with respondent no.2,  Jagarnath
(his nephew) in the year 1990 in respect of
shop B and thus, sub let the same and also
committed  default  in  payment  of  rent
whereupon, the appellants preferred the suit
for ejectment on the ground of sub-letting and
default in payment of rent.
3. The  respondent  no.1,  tenant,
admitted  about  partnership  with  defendant
respondent no.2 yet, all the Courts below have
dismissed the appellants’ suit mainly on the
ground that the respondent no.2, being the
nephew of respondent no.1, is a member of the
family as the respondent no.2 was brought up
since  childhood  by  the  respondent  no.1.
Therefore, a partnership with respondent no.2
would not amount to sub-letting.
4. We  have  heard  learned  senior
counsel for the parties at length and perused

--- Page 196 ---
3
the records.
5. Although,  the  High  Court  has
recorded  a  finding  to  the  above  effect,
however,  considering  the  definition  of
‘family’ in Section 3(g) of the Uttar Pradesh
Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent
and Eviction) Act, 1972 (for short, ‘Act,
1972’),  a  nephew  is  not  included  in  the
definition  of  the  ‘family’.  The  said
definition, as contained in Section 3(g) of
the Act, 1972, is reproduced hereunder for
ready reference:
“(g)  "family",  in  relation  to  a
landlord or tenant of  a  building,
means his or her-
(i) spouse,
(ii) male lineal descendants,
(iii) such parents, grand parents and
any unmarried or widowed or divorced
or judicially separated daughter or
daughter of a male lineal descendant,
as may have been normally residing
with him or her,
and includes, a relation to a
landlord, any female having a legal
right of residence in that building;”

--- Page 197 ---
4
6. On  a  plain  reading  of  the
definition of ‘family’ under Section 3(g) of
the Act, 1972, it is apparent that only the
spouse,  male  lineal  descendants  and  such
parents, grand parents and any unmarried or
widowed or divorced or judicially separated
daughter or daughter of male lineal descendant
residing with him or her, are included in the
definition of ‘family’ under Section 3(g) of
the Act, 1972 with other inclusion of, in
relation to a landlord, any female having a
legal right of residence in that building. A
nephew of landlord or a tenant is, thus, not
included in the definition of ‘family’ under
the Act, 1972.
7. Learned senior counsel appearing
for the respondents has placed reliance on the
judgment rendered by this Court in the case of
K.V. Muthu Versus Angamuthu Ammal, (1997) 2
SCC 53 wherein, a foster son is treated as a
member  of  the  family.  Having  perused  the
judgment rendered in the case of K.V. Muthu
(supra), it is clearly discernible that the
tenant therein had left a Will bequeathing a

--- Page 198 ---
5
life estate in favour of the foster son,
therefore, it is not purely a case of foster
son being treated as the member of the family
but, it was on account of the facts special to
that matter which prevailed upon this Court to
treat the foster son of the tenant as the
member of the family.
8. The present is a case where,
except the fact that  respondent no. 2 was
living with the tenant since childhood, there
is no other special facts which may include a
‘nephew’, by process of interpretation, within
the  sweep  of  definition  of  ‘family’,  as
occurring in Section 3(g) of the Act, 1972.
Reading  a  ‘nephew’  in  the  definition  of
‘family’,  would  amount  to  expanding  the
definition of ‘family’ and if that is allowed,
then this Court would be permitting expansion
of  such  definition  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of a particular case.
9. If the intention of the Legislature
is not to include any other family member in
the definition of ‘family’, than the ones who
are mentioned in the definition of ‘family’,

--- Page 199 ---
6
it is not open for us to include any other
member within the definition of ‘family’.
10. Once, this Court holds that a
‘nephew’ is not a member of the ‘family’, as
defined in Section 3(g) of the Act, 1972, the
other factual basis for seeking eviction of
the respondent nos.1 and 2 from Shop B of the
suit  premises,  is  admitted.  Although,  the
appellants-landlord has sought eviction from
both the premises, i.e. Shop  A and Shop B on
the ground that the tenancy was joint and
common, therefore, once the respondent no.1-
tenant is guilty of sub-letting a part of the
tenanted premises, he deserves to be evicted
from  the  entire  premises.  However,  the
evidence available in the case would suggest
that  Shop  A  and  Shop  B  were  treated
separately all throughout and as a matter of
fact, this is the finding recorded by the
Courts below also.
11. Thus, if the default  qua sub-
letting has occasioned only in respect of
Shop  B,  we  allow  this  appeal  in  part
directing  respondents/  tenants/sub-tenant’s

--- Page 200 ---
7
eviction from Shop B alone.
12. Thus, the impugned order is set
aside  in  part  and  the
respondents/tenants/sub-tenant  are  directed
to handover vacant possession of Shop B to
the appellants within a period of six months
from today subject to usual undertaking being
filed by them in the Registry of this Court
within a period of one week from today. The
respondents/tenants/sub-tenant  shall  also
clear the entire arrears of rent, if any, in
relation to Shop B within one month and shall
also  continue  to  pay  the  current
rent/occupational charges in respect of Shop
B till the time the respondents/ tenants/
sub-tenant vacate the subject premises.
13. In  addition,  the  respondents/
tenants/ sub-tenant shall also not create any
third party interest in the subject tenanted
premises  of  Shop  B  till  the  period  the
respondents/  tenants/  sub-tenant  remain  in
occupation.

--- Page 201 ---
8
14. In the aforestated terms, the
appeal is partly allowed.
15. No  order  as  to  costs
throughout.
........................J.
(PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA)
.......................J.
 (SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR)
New Delhi
