IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.          /2026
[ARISING OUT OF SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL)
NOS.18775-18779/2026]
THE STATE OF KARNATAKA                        APPELLANT(s)
                           VERSUS
RAJ MOHAMMED & ORS.                          RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. These appeals impugn an interim order dated 21.09.2026
by  which  the  High  Court  has  issued  a  slew  of
directions and constituted a Special Investigation
Team (SIT) comprising five IPS Officers to  de novo
investigate the allegations forming the subject matter
of Crime Nos.78 of 2026 and 89 of 2026.
4. On 01.10.2026 after hearing the learned counsel for
the parties, we had passed the following order: 
"1. Having regard to the facts of the case, the
High Court by the impugned order has constituted
a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to investigate
into the subject matter of Crime Nos. 78 of 2026
and 89 of 2026.
2. The State has filed this petition primarily on
the ground that investigation of the aforesaid
cases was nearing completion and there were no
specific allegations against the Investigating
1

--- Page 212 ---
Agency warranting transfer of the investigation
of  the  subject  cases.  Besides,  they  have
objection to the direction contained in paragraph
34 (ii) which requires the SIT to undertake a de
novo investigation.
3. It has been submitted that there was no need
for a de novo investigation, particularly when
there were no allegations of mala fide against
the investigating agency.
4. In addition to above, the State has objection
to some of the members of the SIT constituted by
the High Court.
5. Issue notice, returnable on 12.10.2026.
6. Mr. Sudhanshu Prakash, Advocate accepts notice
on behalf of second respondent.
7. In the meantime, the direction as found in
paragraphs 34 (i) and 34 (ii) of the impugned
order shall remain stayed.
8. By the next date, the State (petitioner) shall
submit in a sealed cover objection, if any,
against the members of the SIT constituted by the
High Court. They may also suggest alternative
names for the SIT."
5. At the outset, we may observe that having regard to
the seriousness of the allegations and possibility of
involvement of functionaries in the Commission, the
case requires investigation by a Special Investigation
Team comprising high ranking officers, therefore, we
do not find a good reason to interfere with the
impugned order insofar as it directs for investigation
by an SIT. 
6. In that context, the learned counsel representing the
appellant-State has confined his challenge to the
composition of the SIT and the direction to conduct de
novo investigation.
7. It  is  urged  that  there  is  no  finding  of  any
investigational lapse or misconduct on the part of the
2

--- Page 213 ---
investigating agency which has investigated the matter
thus  far;  therefore,  in  absence  of  any  finding
regarding investigational lapses or manipulation in
the course of investigation or circumstances which may
suggest  removal  of  evidence,  there  was  no
justification for a de novo investigation.
8. We find substance in the above submission. A de novo
investigation has serious consequences and a direction
in that regard must be issued in rare circumstances
such as where there are allegations of bias/ malice or
serious investigational lapses including removal or
manipulation of evidence. No such finding has been
recorded  in  the  impugned  order.  In  our  view,
therefore,  the  direction  to  conduct  a  de  novo
investigation into the subject crime pertaining to
Crime Nos.78 of 2026 and 89 of 2026 is neither
warranted nor justified.  We, therefore, deem it
appropriate to set aside the direction contained in
paragraph 34(ii) of the impugned order whereunder the
SIT  has  been  directed  to  undertake  a  de  novo
investigation into the subject crime.
9. In respect of the composition of the SIT, we have been
provided certain material wherein the appellant has
shown reasons to have certain reservations about the
3

--- Page 214 ---
person who has been appointed head of the SIT and,
therefore,  they  have  requested  a  change  in  that
regard.  There  are  also  reservations  about  the
Director, Forensic Science Laboratory of the State
being part of the SIT as, according to the State, at
some stage, there may be conflict of interest because
the materials collected during investigation may have
to undergo forensic analysis.
10. In that backdrop, the learned counsel representing the
State has suggested a via media for a change in the
composition of the SIT. According to him, the Director
General of Police, Karnataka should be given liberty
to nominate alternative members, not below the rank of
Additional Director General of Police in the State of
Karnataka, to replace the aforesaid two members.
11. The learned counsel representing the complainant -
respondents, have submitted that if the State is
seeking a change in the composition of the SIT, it
would be appropriate that the State may suggest the
names to the High Court which is seized of the matter
so that it may deliberate upon it and pass appropriate
orders in respect of change in the composition of the
SIT. 
12. The aforesaid suggestion appears reasonable. In such
4

--- Page 215 ---
view of the matter, we deem it appropriate to dispose
of this appeal by setting aside the direction for a de
novo investigation, as found in paragraph 34 (ii) of
the impugned order, and substitute it by directing
that the SIT shall conduct further investigation from
the stage at which the investigation was left by the
previous investigating agency. We further deem it
appropriate to accept the request for change in the
composition of SIT to the extent indicated above.
However, we leave it open to the High Court to
appoint/  substitute  the  Head/  member  in  the  SIT
constituted earlier. To facilitate such appointment/
substitution, the appellant-State shall be at liberty
to suggest alternative names for replacement of the
aforesaid two members in the SIT.  Such alternative
names shall be placed before the High Court within two
weeks from now. Upon receipt of those names, the High
Court shall give opportunity to the other side to
raise their objection, if any. After considering the
objections and hearing both sides, the High Court
shall decide on the alternative names and replace the
aforesaid two members in the SIT.
13. These appeals are disposed of in the above terms. The
impugned order stands modified to the extent indicated
5

--- Page 216 ---
above. 
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(C) No. 29882/2024)
SANDHYARANI NAYAK    APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.             RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. In  the  present  civil  appeal,  the
consideration is limited to the extent of the
Petitioner’s  and  her  husband’s  entitlement  to
disability pension.
3. Ramakant  Nayak,  the  husband  of  the
appellant, was employed as a constable/tailor in
the  Central  Reserve  Police  Force
(‘CRPF’)/respondent No. 2.
4. On  21.10.1994,  Ramakant  Nayak  was
invalidated on medical grounds and discharged from
the service w.e.f. 24.10.1994. The invalidation was
attributed  to  an  electrocution  resulting  in
Traumatic Paraplegia, caused by a fall from a tree.

--- Page 235 ---
2
After prolonged suffering, Ramakant Nayak died on
09.06.2019. During his lifetime, the respondents
sanctioned and paid an invalid pension to the late
Ramakant Nayak. After his demise, the appellant
took  up  the  cause  of  her  husband's  untimely
discharge from service and claimed a disability
pension. The appellant was unsuccessful before the
Writ Court. Hence, the civil appeal. The question
for examination in the civil appeal is whether the
circumstances  surrounding  the  fall  and  the
resultant physical injuries to the late Ramakant
Nayak were attributable to the course of employment
or not, and whether the respondents conducted an
enquiry  or  followed  the  standard  operating
procedure in the present case. The contemporaneous
record is the best evidence either way.
5. We have heard Advocate Ms. Usha Rani Pradhan
for the appellant and learned Additional Solicitor
General Mr. Brijender Chahar for the respondents.
6. We have taken note of the proceedings of the
Board of Medical Officers dated 06.08.1994 and have
perused the record.
7. The incident has occurred within the CRPF
camp premises.

--- Page 236 ---
3
8. Stated  briefly,  the  appellant  attributes
this to an incident occurring while in service as a
constable. However, the respondents join issue on
this.  The  Court,  on  22.09.2026,  passed  the
following order:
“1. At the request of Mr. Brijender
Chahar,  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General,  to  get  instructions  on  the
availability of records and also, without
prejudice to the rights and contentions of
the respondents, to find out a reasonable
lump sum amount that could be paid to the
petitioner for the past claims, and the
family  pension  to  which  the  petitioner
would be entitled, if a case is made out.
2. List on 29.09.2026. “
9. The learned Additional Solicitor General has
been instructed, and considering the issue from
both  a  human  perspective  and  the  respondents'
difficulty in placing the entire record before the
Court, it has been suggested that a lump sum amount
towards the difference in arrears between invalid
pension and disability pension may be considered
and paid to the Petitioner and her husband. Insofar
as the disability pension is concerned, it can be
made effective prospectively.
10. We have taken note of the submissions and
the total arrears payable due to the difference

--- Page 237 ---
4
between these two types of pensions, which works
out to Rs.19,58,273/- (Rupees nineteen lakhs fifty-
eight thousand two hundred and seventy-three). The
appellant, for that matter, or her husband, has not
moved in the matter within a reasonable time,
pressing  for  the  sanction  and  disbursal  of
disability pension. For the delay on the part of
the appellant, we do not propose to impose onerous
conditions  on  the  respondents.  Therefore,  to
balance all aspects of the case, we direct that the
respondents  pay  a  lump  sum  of  Rs.  7,00,000/-
(Rupees seven lakhs only) to the appellants within
three  months  from  today  towards  arrears  of
disability pension.
11. We further direct that the appellant be paid
disability  pension  from  31.05.2026  onwards  and
continue to pay it as per the scheme.
12. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  stands
modified to the above extent. We reiterate that the
instant  order  is  confined  to  deciding  the
entitlement to disability pension and nothing else.
13. The present appeal stands disposed of in the
above terms.

--- Page 238 ---
5
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.          OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRL) NO. 17621 OF 2026]
MAHESH KAUSHAL   …APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH   …RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Appellant, though not arrayed as an accused in the subject
FIR1, was arrested on 6 th December, 2025 and figures as an
accused in a chargesheet 2 filed under Section 193(3) of the
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 for offences under
Sections 103(1), 352, 49, 61(2) and 126(2) of the Bharatiya
Nyay Sanhita, 2023, inter alia, on the allegation that he aided
and facilitated the offence of murder by wrongfully restraining
the deceased from leaving the spot.
1 FIR No. 358 of 2025 dated 20th November, 2025, registered with P .S. Una Sadar
2 Chargesheet no. … dated 13th February, 2026

--- Page 242 ---
2
3. The  prosecution  alleges  that  on  29th September,  2025,  the
deceased-Ashu Puri along with the complainant, the appellant
and several other persons were present outside Hotel Raizada,
upon  celebrating  the  deceased’s  birthday.  Gurjeet  Mann,
Purjinder and Parminder and others approached the group and
an assault ensued. When the group had almost dispersed, the
deceased  and  the  appellant  were  talking  with  each  other.
Parminder then approached the deceased and the appellant
and shot the  deceased from  close  range  with a  pistol.  The
complainant and his companions apprehended the shooter. The
deceased  was  taken  to  the  regional  hospital  where  he  was
pronounced dead. FIR came to be registered against Parminder,
Purjinder and Gurjeet Mann. 
4. Appellant avers that he had no role whatsoever in the entire
crime. In fact, he attempted to save the deceased by shielding
him from the assailant. T o prove this averment, the appellant
has placed on record CCTV footage of the incident.
5. We have perused the CCTV footage and heard learned counsel
for the parties. 
6. Presence  of  the  appellant  at  the  scene  of  crime  and  his
conversation  with  the  deceased  immediately  before  he  was
shot  is  not  disputed.  However,  prima  facie, the  evidence
regarding his plea of shielding the deceased is as inconclusive

--- Page 243 ---
3
as his involvement in aiding or abetting the offence of murder.
The prosecution has to prove at the trial that the appellant was
a conspirator in the murder of the deceased. 
7. Appellant has been in custody for more than 10 (ten) months.
Chargesheet  has  already  been  filed  against  him.  The
prosecution proposes to examine about 49 witnesses. We are
also told that further investigation  qua the other accused is
under way. 
8. T aking  an  overall  view  of  the  matter,  including  the
circumstance that trial will take its own time to conclude, we
are of the considered opinion that the principle of ‘bail being
the rule and jail the exception’ is attracted in the present case
and also that further detention of the appellant pending trial
may not be necessary.
9. Accordingly, we accept the appeal and set aside the impugned
judgment and order. 
10. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to furnishing of bail
bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to such
other terms and conditions as may be imposed by it.
11. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,  directly  or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade
any  person  acquainted  with  the  facts  of  the  case  from
disclosing such facts to the court. 

--- Page 244 ---
4
12. In the event there is any breach of the terms and conditions for
grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty to cancel the bail
of the appellant. 
13. It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellant  shall  diligently  attend
proceedings of the trial, unless exempted. If he abstains from
attending the proceedings without justifiable cause, that could
also be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail and
the trial court will be free to pass appropriate orders. 
14. If the appellant’s interrogation is considered necessary for the
purpose of further investigation, the investigating officer shall
be free to issue notice to him for his appearance at the police
station. Should the appellant not appear, such conduct shall be
treated  as  a  ground  for  cancelling  the  bail  granted  by this
order.
15. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant of
bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case. 

--- Page 245 ---
5
16. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed  on  the  aforesaid  terms.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

    DIPANKAR DATTA

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.             OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.14484 OF 2026)
SUSHILA YADAV ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA ..... RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.             OF 2026
(@SLP(Crl) No. 14463/2026)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. In these appeals the appellants are seeking for grant of anticipatory bail, in
the background of FIR No.75/2026 and 312/2026 registered for the offences
punishable under Sections 406,  420, 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC)
and under Sections 204, 319 and 62 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
(BNS) respectively.
4. The  case  of  the  complainant  is  that  Anil  Yadav and  Sushila  Yadav
representing themselves as owners and competent to sell one acre of land,
situated in village Noorpur, Jharsa, Gurugram had entered into an Agreement to
Sell with the complainant on 23.10.2023 for Rs.9.60 crores and initially paid 40
1

--- Page 254 ---
lakhs  by  cheque  as  earnest  money  and  subsequently  Rs.1  crore  was  paid
through banking channels. The complainant claims further sum of Rs.2 crores
was paid in cash on 02.01.2024 and Rs.3.58 crores in cash on 18.01.2024 and
these payments were acknowledged by the accused to endorsement on the
reverse of the agreement was made. Despite having received these substantial
sale consideration, accused allegedly kept postponing the execution of the Sale
Deed.
5. The prosecution further alleges that material facts concerning acquisition
proceedings of the subject land and the order of status quo related to the
property, had not been disclosed to the purchaser and therefore complainant
had  been  dishonestly  induced  to  enter  into  sale  transaction  with  accused.
During the course of investigation, an additional allegation was made regarding
the purported subsequent altered agreement and offences related to forgery
were  stated  to  have  been  added  on  30.03.2026.  In  this  background,  the
appellants,  who  are  facing  the  criminal  prosecution,  sought  for  grant  of
anticipatory bail contending that dispute is of civil nature.
6. During the pendency of these proceedings, accused is said to have agreed to
execute a memorandum of settlement on 18.05.2026, under which the accused
had agreed to execute the Sale Deed in respect of property agreed to be sold
and accordingly the Sale Deed has been executed on 02.09.2026 (Annexure
A3).
7. In the light of the said settlement arrived at, the continuation of the criminal
prosecution, according to the parties, would only be an exercise in futility and
would not serve any purpose. It is in the teeth of the settlement agreement
entered into between the parties, the accused, namely, the appellants herein,
have  sought  for  quashing  of  the  aforesaid  FIRs,  namely,  FIR  No.75  dated
29.01.2026 and FIR No.312 dated 25.05.2026 and all consequential proceedings
arising thereunder. The learned counsel appearing for the State would submit
2

--- Page 255 ---
that dispute essentially having been settled, appropriate orders may be passed.
8.  Having regard to the aforesaid facts, we are of the considered view that
continuation of further proceedings pursuant to the registration of the two FIRs,
which dispute also carried the flavour of civil dispute, and same having been
settled, continuation of the criminal proceedings would only be an exercise in
futility and it would waste of precious judicial time. As such, we are of the
considered  view  that  said  FIRs  and  all  proceedings  consequential  thereto
deserves  to  be  quashed  in  exercise  of  power  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution of India and in order to do complete justice between the parties
and we do so.
9. Hence, in exercise the power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India
FIR  No.75  dated  29.01.2026  and  FIR  No.312  dated  25.05.2026  are  hereby
quashed  and also the proceedings arising therefrom.
10. In the aforesaid agreement the parties have also agreed as under:
“Civil Suit No.1588 of 2026 dated 06.05.2026, pending on the file
of  District  Judge,  District  Gurugram,  Haryana,  would  also  be
quashed in terms of the settlement that has been entered into
between the parties.” 
  Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the parties would reiterate the same.
Hence their submissions are placed on record.
11. The Criminal Appeals stand disposed of accordingly.

Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C) No.34137/2026

VILE PARLE RAJTARA CHS LIMITED & ORS.            Petitioner(s)

MAHESH MAHENDRABHAI MODI                         Respondent(s)
FOR ADMISSION 
IA No. 311676/2026 - PERMISSION TO FILE ADDITIONAL

Date : 12-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE J.B. PARDIWALA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) :Mrs. Nina R. Nariman, Adv.

--- Page 266 ---
SLP(C) No.34137/2026
                   Mr. S.P. Ojha, Adv.
                   Ms. Princess Singh, Adv.
                                     
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Krishnamohan K.- 2561, AOR
                   Ms. Prerna Jain Kala, Adv.
                   Mr. Vikramjit Garewal, Adv.
                   Mr. Rupesh Geete, Adv.
                   
                   
Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
O R D E R
1. The petitioner Society is aggrieved with the impugned
order of the High Court, which affirmed the interim
injunction granted by the Trial Court. The petitioner was
involved in the redevelopment of a 48-year-old building
and  in  considering  the  reallotment  to  the  present
occupant, the 1st respondent had raised a contention with
respect to his ownership of an Open Terrace. This was
disputed by the Society, upon which a suit was filed, in
which an interim order of injunction was passed. The suit
is pending and we are only concerned with the adjustment
of the equities; in preservation of the rights, if any,
accrued to the plaintiff while not adversely affecting
the redevelopment work.
2

--- Page 267 ---
SLP(C) No.34137/2026
2. We heard Smt. Nina R. Nariman, learned Counsel for
the petitioner and Sri. Krishnamohan K., learned AoR for
the 1st respondent.
3. The specific contention of the plaintiff i.e., the 1st
respondent, was with respect to an ‘Open to Sky’ Terrace
attached to Flat No.B-405, the ownership of the flat
being  admitted  by  the  Society,  as  conferred  on  the
plaintiff.  The  plaintiff  itself  has  relied  on  the
feasibility  report  of  the  Architect,  from  which  an
extract was made in the order of the Trial Court, which
we extract hereunder:
"As per the details forwarded by the Society,
the Open to Sky common Part Terrace adm. 1494
sq.ft. is attached to the adjoining Flat No.
B-405. On verification with the copy of the
certified  Last  approved  Plans  dated
17/05/1998, of the extg. Society building, in
my opinion, as per prevailing Market practice,
the said area of the Open to Sky Terrace
attached to the Flat No.B-405 is adopted to
the extent of 33 % of the said open to Sky
Terrace i.e. 1494 sq.ft x 0.33 = 493 sq.ft."
4. The additional claim is with respect to 493 sq. ft. and
3

--- Page 268 ---
SLP(C) No.34137/2026
we are of the opinion that the equities can be adjusted with
a  direction  to  the  Society  to  design  a  unit  with  the
additional area, as indicated by the Architect and if the
plaintiff is found disentitled in the suit, then either he
would pay the price for the additional area or the Society
could  sell  that  premises  and  provide  him  with  a  unit
commensurate with his entitlement.
5. The Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority
(MHADA) shall provisionally certify the plaintiff’s area as
that of the flat plus the abutting terrace, to the extent the
Architect has provided for. The Society shall ensure that a
unit of that extent shall be constructed in the new building,
which shall be conceded to the plaintiff, if his entitlement
is eventually found; and if not, offer the same to the
plaintiff with a condition of payment being made to the
Society for the additional area with reference to the Open
Terrace. If the petitioner refuses to purchase the same on
his disentitlement being found, the Society could also sell
the said property and provide an alternate accommodation to
the plaintiff commensurate with his actual entitlement.
4

--- Page 269 ---
SLP(C) No.34137/2026
6. We were told by the learned Counsel for the respondent
that even now, the Society has barely been asked to preserve
his right. However, we are at a disadvantage insofar as the
order of the Trial Court only speaks of allowing the prayers
in the Notice of Motion No.1701 of 2024, as prayed for in
Clauses A(i), (ii) and (iii). A copy of the Notice of Motion
has not been produced along with the Special Leave Petition.
It is, hence, we pass the above order ensuring preservation of
the plaintiff’s rights but also facilitating the redevelopment
process. 
7. The  plaintiff  shall  hence  vacate  the  premises  in
accordance with the conditions of redevelopment within a
period of one month or the time provided by the Society to the
other residence, whichever is greater. 
8. We  make  it  clear  that  we  have  not  considered  the
entitlement of the plaintiff for the Open Terrace, which will
be  considered  in  the  suit,  uninfluenced  by  any  of  the
observations made by the High Court or this order.
5

--- Page 270 ---
SLP(C) No.34137/2026
9. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. By our order dated 01.09.2026, we had directed the
States/UTs to take into consideration the deficiencies as
highlighted by us in the order and report in that regard by
the next date of hearing.
4

--- Page 281 ---
2. Today,  when  the  matter  was  taken  up  for  further
hearing, Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, the learned A.S.G submitted
that the Union has taken up this issue very seriously with
all the States/UTs to respond in what manner the judgment
delivered  by  this  Court  is  being  implemented.
Unfortunately, the States/UTs have not responded to the
Union so far.
3. We fail to understand that once the Union calls for the
necessary information, why the States/UTs do not respond.
4. We  are  sure  that  the  Union,  the  States/UTs  have
realized  the  importance  of  the  judgment  that  we  have
delivered, declaring menstrual hygiene as a part of the
Fundamental  Right.  In  other  words,  we  have  declared
menstrual hygiene/ menstrual health as one of the facets of
Article 21 of the Constitution. If what we have said in the
judgment is only going to remain on paper, how is the Union,
States/UTs going to give effect to this Fundamental Right?
5. Whatever we have done, we have done in the interest of
young girls who are giving up education, more particularly,
in remote parts of the country because of the problem of
menstrual hygiene, etc.
6. We  direct  the  Union  to  take  up  this  issue  very
seriously with each of the States/UTs and call for the
necessary information in writing as what steps they have
taken so far for giving effect to the judgment delivered by
this Court.
7. The Union should study the judgment once again and
5

--- Page 282 ---
accordingly call for the information on each and every
aspect of the matter, while giving special attention to
paragraphs 11, 13 to 23, respectively, of our order dated
01.09.2026. 
8. To comply with our directions in paragraph 23, the
Union may prepare a format in the form of questions and seek
appropriate reply from each of the States/UTs.
9. On the next date of hearing, if we hear from the Union
that some of the States/UTs have not responded, we shall
proceed further to issue notice of contempt to the concerned
Chief Secretary of the State(s).
10. We grant one last opportunity to do the needful in the
matter.
11. Post this matter for further hearing on 14 th December,
2026 at 02:30 P.M.
12. We are giving sufficient time to the Union to undertake
this entire exercise.

            IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
   CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.  4886/2026
[Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.16487/2026]
NAVDEEP SINGH                              APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF HARYANA              RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh,
by  the  impugned  judgment  and  order  dated  11th August,
2026,  has  dismissed  the  appellant’s  prayer  for  bail  in
anticipation of arrest. 
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No.0160 dated
07th July,  2026  registered  at  Police  Station  Sadar  Rattia,
District Fatehabad, Haryana under Sections 115, 118(1), 126,
190, 191(2), 191(3), 324(4) & 351(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023.
4. We  have  heard  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
parties and perused the counter-affidavit of the respondent-
State of Haryana.
Crl. Appeals @ SLP (Crl.) No.16487/2026  1

--- Page 290 ---
5. It appears from the counter-affidavit that the appellant
has joined investigation in terms of the earlier order of this
Court and that the police have seized the Swift car bearing
registration  No.  HR-59D-2539,  allegedly  involved  in  the
offence, based on his statement.
6. T aking an overall view of the matter, we are of the
considered  opinion  that  detention  of  the  appellant  for
custodial interrogation is not required and that he  may be
admitted to an order for grant of bail in anticipation of arrest.
7. We,  accordingly,  set  aside  the  judgment  and  order
impugned in this appeal.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

CRIMINAL APPEAL No.   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No.14669/2026)
ROHIT VERMA ..... APPELLANT(S)
            
               VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3.  Appellant is aggrieved by the order dated 20.11.2025,
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) rejecting the bail
application of the appellant. 
4.  Appellant is an accused in Case Crime No. 0134 of
2025, registered at Police Station Kotwali, District
Jhansi (Uttar Pradesh) for the offences punishable under
Sections  80(2),  85,  115(2),  352  and  351(3)  of  the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), read with Sections 3
and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
5. According to the prosecution, appellant is the husband
of  the  deceased.  Their  marriage  was  solemnised  on
1

--- Page 305 ---
14.03.2023. Deceased was subjected to cruelty and demand
for dowry. On 25.04.2025, deceased was found dead in her
matrimonial home in hanging position pursuant to which
the  father  of  the  deceased,  being  the  de  facto
complainant, lodged the FIR on 27.04.2025, whereafter
appellant came to be arrested on 29.04.2025. Since then,
the appellant has been in custody.
6. This Court, by order dated 06.08.2026, had issued
notice, pursuant to which the respondent-State of Uttar
Pradesh has filed counter affidavit.
7. In the proceedings held on 28.09.2026, the following
order came to be passed:
 1. Mr. Arup Banerjee, learned counsel
for the State of Uttar Pradesh to inform us
on the next date status of the trial; the
number of prosecution witnesses proposed to
be examined and how many have been examined
till date; next date of hearing etc. We take
note of the fact that appellant is in custody
since 29.04.2025.
2. List on 13.10.2026.
8. Pursuant to the aforesaid order, the respondent-State
of Uttar Pradesh has filed a supplementary affidavit,
which we have perused. In paragraph 3 of the said
affidavit, it is stated that the prosecution intends to
examine 27 witnesses to prove its case. As of today, the
examination-in-chief  of  PW-1,  i.e.,  father  of  the
deceased has taken place but he is yet to be cross-
2

--- Page 306 ---
examined.  There  are  26  more  witnesses  left  to  be
examined. 
9. While there is no doubt that the deceased died under
unnatural circumstances in her matrimonial home within
seven years of her marriage, however, we are conscious of
the fact that appellant has been in custody for almost
one and a half years. Moreover, having regard to the
number of witnesses yet to be examined, it will take some
time for the trial court to conclude the trial.
10. That being the position, we are of the view that the
appellant may be enlarged on bail.
11. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order passed
by the High Court dated 20.11.2025 and direct that the
appellant shall be produced before the trial court within
a maximum period of seven days from today, whereafter he
shall be enlarged on bail on such terms and conditions as
may be deemed appropriate.
12. The appeal is allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

     IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
     CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
      CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
     (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 16306/2026)
DEBANSU  SARKAR            APPELLANT
VERSUS
STATE OF ODISHA                                  RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. The  appellant  is  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated
04.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Orissa at Cuttack
(briefly, ‘the High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the bail
application of the appellant.
4. The  appellant  has  been  named  as  an  accused  in
Malkangiri PS Case No. 455/2025 (corresponding to Special
G.R. Case No. 112/2025) pending in the Court of learned
Additional Sessions Judge-cum-Special Judge, Malkangiri,
under Sections 20(b)(ii)(C)/25/29 of the Narcotic Drugs and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (briefly, the ‘NDPS Act’
hereinafter).
@ SLP (CRL.) NO. 16306/2026    1

--- Page 320 ---
5. The prosecution case in brief is that on 30.08.2025,
at about 10:30 A.M., during the checking of vehicles,
100kgs of  ganja  were recovered from a vehicle bearing
registration no. CG 04 HC 3921.  The occupants of the
vehicle, Lala Yadab, Lalji Rajvar and Golok Biswas were
apprehended.  In the course of their interrogation, they
disclosed  that  the  contraband  was  supplied  by  the
appellant.
6. On the basis of the disclosure statement(s), appellant
came to be arrested on 28.11.2025 and has been in custody
since then.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant, at the outset, has
referred to the counter affidavit filed by the State and
submits that no recovery of the contraband was made from
the appellant.  He has been implicated only on the basis of
the disclosure statement(s) of the accused persons.  He is
also not the owner of the vehicle, from which the seizure
was made.
7.1.  Learned counsel for the appellant has also drawn the
attention of the Court to the arrest memo of the appellant
dated 28.11.2026 where against the grounds of arrest, it is
simply mentioned that appellant is involved in the above
noted case. Pleading his innocence, learned counsel for the
appellant prays for his bail.
@ SLP (CRL.) NO. 16306/2026    2

--- Page 321 ---
8. Per  contra,  learned  State  counsel  submits  that
appellant has a criminal antecedent also involving the same
provisions of the NDPS Act.  In that case, seizure of ganja
was made from the appellant himself along with the three
other persons, from an auto rickshaw. However, he was
released on bail by the learned Special Judge under Section
167(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.)
because  of  failure  to  file  chargesheet  within  the
stipulated period.  He submits that appellant has failed to
meet the stipulations of Section 37 of the NDPS Act and,
therefore, he may not be granted bail.
9. The  submissions  made  by  learned  counsel  for  the
parties have received the due consideration of the Court.
On a query by the Court, learned State counsel has informed
that though the chargesheet was submitted, charges have not
yet been framed and, therefore, the trial has not yet
commenced.  However, trial is going on in the case of the
previous antecedent of the appellant.
10. Be that as it may, having regard to the fact that the
appellant is in custody for almost one year and moreover,
considering the fact that no specific ground(s) of arrest
have been mentioned, we are inclined to grant bail to the
appellant.  Merely saying that appellant is involved in the
case is not sufficient to meet the requirement of Clause
(1) of Article 22 of the Constitution of India.
@ SLP (CRL.) NO. 16306/2026    3

--- Page 322 ---
11. In  such  circumstances,  we  are  of  the  considered
opinion that the appellant deserves to be enlarged on bail.
12. Consequently, we set aside the impugned order of the
High Court dated 04.05.2026 and direct that the appellant
shall be produced before the learned Special Judge within a
maximum period of seven days from today, whereafter, he
shall be enlarged on bail on such terms and conditions as
may deem appropriate.
13.  Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
14.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

…………………………………………………...J.
        [ATUL S. CHANDURKAR]
NEW DELHI;

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant has been arraigned as an accused
and seeks regular bail in connection with FIR
No.343/2021, registered at Police Station - B
Division, District – Amritsar, and has been
charge-sheeted for the offences punishable under
Sections 302, 307, 34, 108, 120-B, 111, 112 and
201 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 as well as
Sections 25, 27, 54 and 59 of the Arms Act, 1959
3. We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing for the appellant and the learned
1

--- Page 325 ---
counsel appearing for the respondent(s).
4. Out of the total number of 54 witnesses, 18
witnesses have been examined. The case of the
prosecution  against  the  appellant  is  that,
pursuant  to  the  disruption  caused  in  the
relationship between the appellant and another
person,  a  conspiracy  was  hatched  by  the
appellant who hired the co-accused and committed
the offence. 
5. Learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant submitted that the appellant has been
under incarceration for nearly 5 years. Only 18
out of 54 witnesses have been examined and,
hence,  the  trial  would  take  more  time  to
conclude.  There  is  no  adequate  material  to
implicate the appellant.
6. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent
submits that the evidence available would show
that the appellant is the mastermind who hatched
a conspiracy, hired the co-accused and committed
the offence. 
7. Suffice  it  to  state  that  the  period  of
incarceration  of  the  appellant  is  not  in
dispute. The trial is proceeding at a slow pace.
2

--- Page 326 ---
According to the prosecution, it is a case of
mistaken identity in killing the deceased.
8. Taking note of the above, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order passed by the High
Court, and grant regular bail to the appellant.
9. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  stands  set
aside, and the appellant is granted regular
bail, subject to the terms and conditions that
may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court.
10. The  concerned  Trial  Court  is  directed  to
expedite the trial and make an endeavour to
conclude the same within a period of four months
from the date of receipt of a copy of this
order.  
11. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Our order dated 08.09.2025 reads thus:
“1. We heard this matter for almost half an hour.
2. We are highly disturbed with some facts.
3. Here is a case wherein a 10-year-old girl is
being traumatised like anything in a legal battle
between her father and mother.
2

--- Page 336 ---
4. We give one last chance to the parties to sit,
talk and reach to some understanding by which the
interest of the minor daughter is protected in all
respects. The nature of the allegations levelled by
the parties against each other is something beyond
our imagination. We are inclined to put to an end
all the proceedings between the parties, civil as
well  as  criminal,  and  further  work  out  some
modalities by which the mother has a chance to
visit her daughter once or twice in a month.
5. We are saying this because there are final
orders passed by the courts, including this Court,
directing the mother to hand over the custody of
the minor daughter to the father. Today, we are
dealing with a Contempt Petition filed by the
father.
6. We humbly request both the sides to work out
something which would be in the absolute interest
of the minor daughter.
7. Post this matter on 23.09.2025 on top of the
board.
8. We make it clear that by 23.09.2025 if something
is worked out, then well and good, otherwise we
shall  proceed  to  pass  appropriate  orders  in
accordance with law.”
We take notice of the fact that last year,
this Court, to which one of us K.V. Vishwananathan,
J. was a part of the Bench had an occasion to
interact with the parties including the minor girl.
The record reveals that the interaction had taken
place on 01.10.2024.
Almost a period of one year has elapsed. 
We are of the view that we should have one
more round of interaction with the parties. 
3

--- Page 337 ---
We direct the parties to personally remain
present on 16.10.2025 at 02:00 p.m. We shall talk
to the parties in the Committee Room. We request
the parties to keep the minor girl present on that
day.
List on 16.10.2025 as part-heard.
  (KRITIKA TIWARI)                                (POOJA SHARMA)

         UPON hearing the counsel the Court made 
the following
                      O R D E R
1. The petitioner has been denied anticipatory
bail  by  courts  below  in  connection  with  FIR
No.237/2024  dated  22.10.202 4  registered  with
Vasant Kunj North Police Station , District South
West, New Delhi, for the offence punishable under
Sections 420, 468, 471 and 34 respectively, of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860.
2. The petitioner is accused of fraudulently
inducing the complainant to transfer substantial
amounts  on  false  pretext  of  settling  company
liabilities,  diverting  the  funds  for  personal
benefit,  and  deceiving  the  complainant  by
presenting  an  allegedly  forged  document.  The
petitioner was denied anticipatory bail by the
High  Court  on  the  ground  that  detailed
investigation into alleged diversion of funds and
other  connected  issues  required  custodial
SLP (Crl.) No.19130/2026 2

--- Page 348 ---
interrogation. 
3. In the facts and circumstances of this case

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO(S).  11297/2016
K.V. SEETHARAMAN PRESIDENT OF 
KULITHALAL NAIDU MAHAJAN SANGAM APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
THE ASSTISTANT COMMISSIONER H.R. 
AND C.E. ADMIN DEPT. & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
appellant and the learned Senior counsel appearing for the
respondents. 
2. The appellant herein instituted a suit in the year 1988, for
declaration of the right to manage and administer the affairs
of  Sri  Venugopalswamy  Bajanaimadam  and  for  consequential
injunction, which was decreed by the Trial Court vide order
dated 18.09.1995. The High Court, vide order dated 16.12.2009,
in an appeal by the respondents reversed the findings of the
Trial  Court,  by  holding  that  the  suit  itself  was  not
maintainable in the absence of a declaration having been
obtained from the Deputy Commissioner under Section 63(a) of
the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act,
1959 (hereinafter 'the said Act').

--- Page 363 ---
2
3. In the present case, the short issue involved is, as to
whether the judgment and decree of the High Court in holding
that the suit is not maintainable is proper or not. 
4. While concurring with the High Court's conclusion, we are
inclined to hold that there is no need for incidental findings
on facts. In fact the appellant did invoke Section 63(a) of
the said Act, which was dismissed on default. Suffice it is to
state, that in view of the judgment of the High Court, there
is no bar for the appellant to invoke Section 63(a) of the
said Act once again, particularly, by taking note of the fact
that the earlier application was dismissed on default. 
5. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to grant six weeks
time to the appellant from the date of receipt of a copy of
this order to invoke Section 63(a) of the said Act. 
6. Such application being filed before the concerned authority
namely, Joint/Deputy Commissioner, shall be disposed of within
a period of three months thereafter. Till such time, status
quo as of today, shall be maintained by the parties.
7. We make it clear that the competent authority is directed to
decide the application on its own merits and in accordance
with the law, without being influenced by any of the findings
on merit rendered by the High Court in the impugned judgment. 
8. The appeal stands disposed of, in the aforesaid terms and with
aforementioned directions. 

--- Page 364 ---
3
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
    
  ……………………………………………………………………J.
  [M.M. SUNDRESH]
       ………………………………………………………………………J.
[PRASANNA B. VARALE]

KARTHI ALIAS KARTHIKEYAN                           PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
STATE REP BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE                   RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. There is an inordinate delay of 980 days in filing this
review petition.  However, we have still gone through the
review petition and also the documents enclosed. 
2. One of the grounds raised by the review petitioner is

--- Page 375 ---
2
that he was sentenced to 20 years by the Trial Court for the
offence under Section 376D of the IPC, 1860, but the amendment
prescribing 20 years of sentence was subsequently introduced.
3. Having perused the amendment, the date of occurrence and
the sentence imposed, it is clear that the amendment came into
force on 03.02.2013, while the occurrence in the instant case
was of the date 28.10.2103, which is more than 8 months after
the said amendment was brought in. 
4. Hence, we do not find any good ground and reason to
review the order dated 19.10.2023 on merits as well.
5. Accordingly, the review petition is dismissed on the
ground of delay, as well as on merits.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1

--- Page 399 ---
                   
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA No. 62217/2024
1. Heard.
2. The FIR No. 118/2013 came to be registered on 23.06.2013 at Patharkandi
Police Station, Assam, under Sections 147, 148, 341 and 302 of the IPC against
six accused persons. The informant is the widow of the deceased.
3. The brief case of the prosecution is that on 22.06.2013 the deceased
received a call on his mobile at around 7.30 AM regarding purchase of firewood
from his shop and at around 8:00 AM the deceased left his house. After a while,
the informant along with her brother-in-law-Fakar Uddin, also came out from
their house to visit the Doctor.  After going for about half a kilometer of walking
from  their  house,  she  saw the  deceased being  attacked by the  miscreants
armed with sharp weapons and they rushed towards the spot, where accused
no.1-Md. Jakir Hussain, was attacking the deceased by inflicting injury on his
neck with a sharp weapon, namely, a Dao and after which the deceased fell to
the ground.
4. It was further alleged that seven to eight persons including Md. Jakir
Hussain assaulted her husband. Another accused, Moinul Hoque also inflicted
injury on the throat of the informant’s husband with a Dao, when she and her
brother-in-law raised an alarm due to which accused persons ran away. After
investigation a chargesheet came to be filed and trial took place. The Sessions
Court by judgment dated 26.11.2018 acquitted the accused by arriving at a
conclusion that there was manipulation in the case diary; testimonies of the
prosecution  witnesses  fall  apart;  non-examination  of  Mr.  Azizur  Rehman  as
witness during investigation and during the trial, raises a suspicion that he
2

--- Page 400 ---
would not have told the story favouring the prosecution; and, Exhibit-1 was not
the  original  and  the  informant  and  prosecution  witnesses  have  falsely
implicated the accused in the crime and thereby acquitted them.
5. The informant filed an appeal before the High Court amd the jurisdictional
High Court by judgment dated 02.02.2024 reversed the same on the ground
that witnesses have clearly deposed that there was an attack on the deceased
and the accused were seen by them fleeing away from the scene of crime; the
evidentiary value of the FIR is used as a substantive piece of evidence and be
used  as  a  previous  statement  for  the  purpose  of  corroboration;  and  the
evidence tendered by the prosecution was not properly appreciated. Hence, the
Appellate Court on re-appreciation of evidence is said to have set right the
alleged or purported error that had crept in the judgment. 
6. It is the contention of the learned counsel appearing for the appellants
that prima facie High Court decision lacks findings qua the appellants and the
Court failed to appreciate the evidence placed before it and particularly, the
contradictions in the statements of the eye-witnesses; she would also further
elaborate her submissions by contending that High Court failed to consider the
fact that brother of the deceased had informed the police that unknown persons
had killed the deceased and body was thrown near a rivulet in the Ratanpur
village, who was not examined and this raises a serious doubt in prosecution
story and as such she prays for grant of bail. 
7. Per contra, the learned counsel appearing of the respondent-State has
vehemently opposed the grant of the bail by contending that on reappreciation
of evidence the Appellate Court has convicted the accused and as such there is
a presumption of the guilt having been proved and as such he contends that
appellants are not entitled for grant of bail. He would also draw the attention of
the Court to the reply affidavit filed to the prayer for grant of bail to contend
3

--- Page 401 ---
that appellants had indulged in certain illegal activities inside the prison and as
such they are not entitled for the equitable relief.
8. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties and on perusal
of the records, it requires to be noticed at the outset itself that the alleged
incident occurred on 22.06.2013 and the postmortem of the deceased was also
conducted  on  the  same  day  at  1:20  PM.  Surprisingly,  the  FIR  came  to  be
registered on 23.06.2013 at 1:30 PM. In fact, the prosecution itself admits that
cousin of the deceased had telephoned the jurisdictional police informing the
police of the death of the deceased on 22.06.2013, yet, his statement was not
recorded during the course of the investigation nor was he examined during the
trial.
9. It is these loopholes in the prosecution story which swayed in the mind of
the learned Sessions Judge to acquit the accused, also taking note of several
contradictions pointed in its judgment. However, the Appellate Court seems to
have been swayed by the evidence of PW1 and much reliance has been placed.
Same requires scrutiny by this Court.
10. For the aforesaid reasons the matter requires examination and as such
the  trial  Court  records  have  been  summoned  for  examining  the  appeal  on
merits. In the light of divergent findings and the aforestated facts, we are of the
considered  view  that  appellants  are  entitled  for  being  released  on  bail.
Accordingly, the I.A. No. 62217/2024 stands allowed. The jurisdictional Sessions
Court would be at liberty to impose such conditions as it deems fit for release of
the appellants on bail as ordered by this Court.
(DEEPANSHU)                                     (AVGV RAMU)
SENIOR PERSONAL ASSISTANT                     COURT MASTER (NSH)

came only by way of a supplementary statement.  Learned
counsel further submits that the petitioner has already
undergone 3 years and 2 months in custody; out of total

           SLP (Criminal) No.14249/2026 Page 2 of 3

examined so far; and the trial is likely to take a long

for the petitioner under Section 307 of the IPC but

6. Having  perused  the  records;  considered  all  the
submissions made; keeping in mind the period undergone;
and the fact that the trial will take time to conclude,

Court.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 19077-19079 OF 2026)
ITE DESIGNS PVT LTD & ANR. APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
HARISH CHANDRA (INDIA) LIMITED     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant(s) has approached this Court being
aggrieved by the common impugned order dated 25.08.2026
passed by the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in CRL. M.C.
No. 1682 of 2011, CRL. M.A. No. 1332 of 2025 and CRL.M.A.
No. 1333 of 2025.
3. The appellant(s) had preferred a petition under
Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 seeking
quashment of criminal proceedings, wherein an interim order
was initially granted in his favor. Subsequently, the said
petition was dismissed for want of prosecution.
4. The appellant(s) thereafter moved an application for
restoration of the petition along with an application
seeking condonation of delay. The High Court, however,
dismissed the application for condonation of delay and
consequently rejected the restoration application.
1

--- Page 485 ---
5. Learned counsel for the respondent has vehemently
argued that no sufficient cause was shown to explain the
delay and, therefore, the High Court was fully justified in
dismissing the application.
6. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, this
Court is of the opinion that since the matter was never
decided on merits, the appellant(s) deserves an opportunity
to have his petition adjudicated on merits.
7. Accordingly, impugned order passed by the High Court
is set aside and CRL. M.C. No. 1682 of 2011 is restored to
the file of the High Court for consideration on merits,
subject  to  payment  of  costs  of  Rs.25,000/-  by  the
appellant(s) to the respondent.
8. The appeal(s) is allowed in the above terms.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We heard this matter for almost half an hour.
2. We are highly disturbed with some facts.
3. Here is a case wherein a 10-year-old girl is being traumatised

--- Page 516 ---
like anything in a legal battle between her father and mother.
4. We give one last chance to the parties to sit, talk and reach
to some understanding by which the interest of the minor daughter
is protected in all respects.  The nature of the allegations
levelled by the parties against each other is something beyond our
imagination.  We are inclined to put to an end all the proceedings
between the parties, civil as well as criminal, and further work
out some modalities by which the mother has a chance to visit her
daughter once or twice in a month.
5. We are saying this because there are final orders passed by
the courts, including this Court, directing the mother to hand over
the custody of the minor daughter to the father. Today, we are
dealing with a Contempt Petition filed by the father.  
6. We humbly request both the sides to work out something which
would be in the absolute interest of the minor daughter.
7. Post this matter on 23.09.2025 on top of the board.
8. We make it clear that by 23.09.2025 if something is worked
out, then well and good, otherwise we shall proceed to pass
appropriate orders in accordance with law.

CORAM :

For Respondent(s) :Mr. Shrirang B. Varma, Adv.

                   Mr. Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar- 1729, AOR

                   Ms. Usha Bhaskar, Adv.                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr.  Sandeep Sudhakar Deshmukh, learned counsel 
for   the   petitioner, Mr. Shrirang B. Varma, learned
1

--- Page 518 ---
counsel  for  the  State  and  Mr.  Nishant  Ramakantrao
Katneshwarkar, learned counsel for the de facto complainant.
2. The present petition calls in question the correctness of
the order dated 13-07-2026 in BA No. 1149/2026 passed by the
High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad. By
the said order, the petitioner has been denied the benefit of
bail in connection with FIR No.98/2026 registered with City
Chowk Police Station, District Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar for
the offences punishable under Sections 109(1), 118(1), 191(2),
191(3), 115(2), 351(2), 189(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the  
petitioner has undergone almost six months in custody. The 
incident is of 26.03.2026 and the Medical Certificate which 
was contemporaneously issued only showed two simple injuries.
Learned counsel  submits that  the prosecution  which is  
relying on the certificate issued by the Asian Hospital on 
11.04.2026  showing  a  scalp  injury,  which  is  seriously  
disputed. 
4. Learned counsel for the State and learned counsel for the
de facto complainant vehemently opposed the bail. Mr. Shrirang
B. Varma, learned counsel submits that the  CCTV incident  
captures the involvement of the petitioner in the assault of  
26.03.2026. 
5. Mr.  Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar, learned counsel 
submits that after notice was issued in this Special leave 
Petition, the complainant has registered a non-cognizable case
2

--- Page 519 ---
against the father of the petitioner on 24.08.2026 for  
coercing and threatening the petitioner to arrive at a  
settlement.
6. In response, learned counsel for the petitioner submits
that if the non-cogzinable offence case was true, the  
petitioner’s father for the same incident as the present one 
would  not  have  been  enlarged  on  anticipatory  bail  on  
14.09.2026.
7. Having considered the overall facts and circumstances of 
the case and the period of imprisonment undergone, we are 
inclined to enlarge the petitioner on bail, hence, the prayer 
of the petitioner is allowed.
8. Accordingly, we direct that the petitioner be enlarged on 
bail subject to the satisfaction of the concerned Trial Court 
in connection with the aforesaid case(s) for the offences  
mentioned hereinabove. However, considering the fact  that the
de facto complainant has lodged a non-cognizable case, the 
Trial Court may impose stringent conditions as it may deem 
fit.
9. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the above 
terms.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed 
of.
(NEETU SACHDEVA)                                (NIKITA SINGH)
DEPUTY REGISTRAR                               COURT MASTER (NSH)

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This application seeking restoration of Civil Appeal
Diary No.5988 of 2026 has been found prima facie not
1

--- Page 521 ---
maintainable by the learned Chamber Judge vide order
dated 16.07.2026 in view of the decision of this
Court in CA Ramchandra Dallaram Choudhary vs. Adani
Infrastructure and Developers Private Limited.
2. The learned counsel for the appellant/applicant has
cited before us a judgment of this Court dated
28.07.2026 in Civil Appeal No.8807 of 2026 in the
case of Walchandnagar Industries Limited vs Swaraj
India Agro Ltd. wherein it was observed that the
decision in CA Ramchandra Dallaram Choudhary (supra)
would not be applicable to a case where defects are
notified  multiple  times  thereby  giving  fresh
opportunities to cure the defects.
3. The learned Solicitor General who appears for the
respondent  submits  that  decision  in  Walchandagar
Industries Limited (supra) would not be applicable
where  same  defects  are  notified.   Besides,  the
defects must be cured within a specified period from
the date they are notified as was in the case of
Walchandnagar Industries Limited (supra).
4. Our attention has been invited to the defect sheet
of the concerned appeal which finds place in Volume-
VI of I.A. No.258133 of 2026.  By pointing out the
entry at Sl.No.16, it has been submitted on behalf
of the respondents that defects pointed earlier were
again  notified  on  23.06.2025.   In  such
2

--- Page 522 ---
circumstances, the peremptory order of this Court
which mentions that if defects are not cured the
appeal shall stand dismissed would operate and,
therefore, the present case would be distinguishable
from  the  case  handled  by  this  Court  in
Walchandnagar Industries Limited
5. The learned counsel for the applicant has sought to
argue that the entry in the defect sheet at Sl.No.16
is incorrect insofar as it recites that Defect No.3,
4 and 8 along with Defect No.11 were not cured.
6. Having regard to the peculiar facts of the case, we
deem it appropriate to grant time to the applicant
to submit an affidavit raising its objection to the
correctness of the defect sheet prepared by the
Registry.  Such objection/affidavit be filed within
two weeks. The affidavit so filed shall specifically
indicate whether the defects notified earlier were
removed, if so when.
7. The affidavit shall also describe the nature of the
defects and the manner in which they were removed.
In case such an affidavit is filed within the time
specified  above,  the  Registry  would  have  three
weeks’ time to submit a response to the affidavit. 
8. List this matter on 09.12.2026.

Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This petition calls in question the correctness of
the impugned order dated 07 th July, 2025 passed in D.B.
Civil Miscellaneous Appeal No.5748/2017 by the High Court
of Judicature for Rajasthan (Bench at Jaipur).  By the said
order, the High Court has allowed the appeal preferred by
the respondent-husband and set aside the order and decree
dated 25.09.2017 passed by the Family Court, Jaipur in Case
1

--- Page 545 ---
No.810/2017 (193/2004), consequent to which, the marriage
between the parties stood dissolved by a decree of divorce.
2. We  have  heard  Mr.  Shyam  Singh  Chauhan,  learned
counsel appearing for the petitioner-wife, and Mr. Pallav
Shishodia,  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent-husband. 
3. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and
considering the fact that the marriage between the parties
was solemnized in the year 1994 and the parties have been
indisputably living separately for nearly 25 years, we are
prima facie, not inclined to interfere with the impugned
order passed by the High Court.
4. However,  insofar  as  the  permanent  alimony  is
concerned, the High Court has not made any separate orders
for maintenance/ alimony.  It is not disputed that the
respondent-husband had been paying Rs.4,000/- per month
from 2005 to 2015 and Rs.8,500/- per month from 2015 till
date. 
5. Today, we have persuaded the parties to settle the
matter at any consolidated sum which will be towards full
and final settlement against all the dues payable to the
petitioner.  
6. After exchange of some arguments, the parties arrived
at a broad consensus that the respondent-husband shall pay
a sum of Rs. 11,00,000/- (Rupees Eleven Lakhs).  We make it
2

--- Page 546 ---
clear that the aforesaid amount will be towards full and
final settlement of all the claims due and payable to the
petitioner-wife.
7. Based on the consensus, we direct that the aforesaid
amount of Rs.11,00,000/- (Rupees Eleven Lakhs) will be paid
by the respondent-husband in three installments in the
following manner: 
i. First installment of Rs.3,00,000/- (Rupees Three
Lakhs) to be paid on or before 12.11.2026;
ii. Second installment of Rs.3,00,000/- (Rupees Three
Lakhs) to be paid on or before 11.12.2026; and
iii. Final installment of Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees Five
Lakhs) to be paid on or before 11.01.2027. 
8. We make it clear that the respondent-husband shall
continue to pay monthly maintenance of Rs.8,500/- till the
month of January, 2027. 
9. List  the  matter  for  recording  compliance  on
22.01.2027. 
10. In the meantime, other proceedings pending between
the parties, shall be kept in abeyance. 
 (SHUBHAM SONI)                                 (NIKITA SINGH)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
1

--- Page 593 ---
                             O R D E R
SLP(Crl) No. 1612/2026
1. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties.
2. On  18.04.2012  a  mob  comprising  24  persons  allegedly  attacked
deceased Sindura Jani and his family at village Khandikanpa due to the political
rivalry and land disputes, which resulted in deaths of Sindura Jani and his son
Santosh Jani and another son Sushanta sustaining grievous injuries. An FIR No.
54/2012 came to be registered on 19.04.2012 at Manamunda Police Station,
District Boudh, Orissa. Upon completion of the investigation, chargesheet has
been filed and only seven accused persons were arraigned as accused.
3. The learned Sessions Judge, by judgment dated 19.05.2017 convicted all
the  accused  persons.  The  High  Court  in  Criminal  Appeal  No.  378  of  2017
affirmed the judgment of the trial Court. Hence, the present appeal.
4. Petitioners are seeking for grant of bail on the ground of parity. This Court
while examining the prayer of Dibakar Jani @ Thupudi and Kailash Jani had
taken note of the fact that they had completed more than 11 years of sentence
as against the life imprisonment imposed on them. The petitioners herein have
undergone more than 12 years 9 months and 13 years 2 months, respectively
and as such it cannot be gainsaid by the prosecution that petitioners are not
entitled for the relief on the ground of parity. Hence, on that short ground,
without going into the merits of the case, we order for release of the petitioners
by granting bail.
5. Accordingly, the IA No.292377/2026 seeking grant of bail is allowed. The
jurisdictional Court is at liberty to impose such terms and conditions as it deems
2

--- Page 594 ---
fit for enlarging the petitioners on bail.
(DEEPANSHU)                                     (AVGV RAMU)

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SANJEEV SACHDEVA
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Avneesh Arputham, AOR
                    Mr. Ankit Sharma, Adv.
                   
For Respondent(s) :  
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The application bearing IA No. 305370/2026 is
filed on behalf of the petitioner no.1 seeking leave
to file the Transfer Petition. 
2. It is noticed that the petitioner no.1 is not a
party to the suit, transfer of which is sought.
3. Accordingly, the Transfer Petition having been
filed at the behest of the petitioner no.1 is not

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN

                   Mr. Saurav Kumar, Adv.

For Respondent(s) :

                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. We  heard  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioner-convict.
3. It appears from the materials on record that the
petitioner was put to trial in the Court of I st  Additional
Sessions Judge, Saraipali, District Mahasamund, State of
Chhattisgarh in Sessions Trial No.29 of 2021 for the offence
1

--- Page 684 ---
punishable under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (for
short, ‘the IPC’).
4. At the end of the trial, the Trial Court held the
petitioner guilty of the alleged crime and sentenced him to
undergo life imprisonment with fine.
5. The petitioner went in appeal before the High Court.
The High Court, as usual, in a very slipshod manner and
without any understanding of law partly allowed the appeal
by altering the conviction from Section 302 to Section 304
Part II of the IPC.
6. It appears, High Court overlooked the nature of the
injuries sustained by the deceased, the weapon of offence
used for the commission of the crime and also the genesis of
the occurrence.
7. Let notice be issued to the petitioner, calling upon
him to show cause as to why the order of the High Court
should not be set aside and the judgment and order passed by
the Trial Court holding him guilty of the offence of murder
should not be restored. This part we shall consider having
regard to the overall merits of the case.
8. Issue notice to the petitioner as well as to the State
of Chhattisgarh, returnable on 18.11.2026.
9. Dasti service, in addition, is permitted.

against the petitioners by the Court concerned.
3. The High Court, in para 7 of the impugned order has

the order or till the time of surrender of the applicants

--- Page 688 ---

petitioners to appear before the Court concerned, furnish

1. Exemption Applications are allowed.
2. The petitioner challenged the rejection of his bail
application by the High Court in connection with FIR No. 110
of 2026 dated 14.04.2026 registered with Police Station Ganj,
District Raipur, Chhattisgarh for the offence punishable under
Section 7 of the Chhattisgarh Gambling (Prohibition) Act,
2022.              
3. Charge-sheet No.102 of 2026 was filed on 10.06.2026,

--- Page 1202 ---
2
including Section 112(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
Petitioner is named in the charge-sheet as Accused No.27 and
was arrested on 17.04.2026.
4. The petitioner is accused of being involved in an organized
online gambling group, which runs online cricket betting
through  an  app  called  “3  Stumps”,  based  on  disclosure
statements of co-accused.
5. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that several
co-accused have been granted bail by this court. It was
further submitted that the petitioner is not named in the FIR;
implication  was  based  on  alleged  disclosure  statements;
investigation is admittedly complete; and there is delay in
trial, since 38 witnesses are to be examined. 
6. On a prima facie consideration of the material on record,
we are of the opinion that the petitioner can be released on
bail, subject to terms and conditions that the jurisdictional
Court (Judicial Magistrate of the First Class, Raipur) may
deem fit to impose.
7. Ordered accordingly. 
8. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.

of.
